title: Video Streaming (YouTube-style)
problem: Design a video upload, transcoding, and streaming platform like YouTube.
summary: A massively read-skewed system (~99% reads, 1% uploads) split into two flows: a video-uploading flow (original storage → transcoding servers → transcoded storage → CDN, with a completion queue + handler that updates metadata once encoding finishes) and a streaming flow that serves adaptive-bitrate manifests and segments from the CDN with fallback to the transcoded origin. The dominant design choice is push all playback traffic to CDN edge — the origin should see <1% of global playback QPS — while transcoding runs asynchronously on a DAG of tasks (inspection → video encoding → audio encoding → thumbnails → watermark → assembler) so uploads never block on the 10+ minute encode. The main tradeoffs are storage blow-up (each source becomes 6–8 adaptive-bitrate ladders, ~3–5x raw storage) and upload latency, which the book attacks with GOP-level chunk parallelism and upload points geographically near users.

functional: Upload source videos up to multi-GB with resumable, chunked PUTs
Transcode each source into an ABR ladder (240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) plus HLS/DASH segments and thumbnails
Serve adaptive-bitrate playback with sub-second startup and mid-stream ladder switching
Metadata lookup by video ID: title, owner, privacy, length, ladder manifest URL
Trending, recommended, and search surfaces powered by view logs
Content moderation, takedown, and geo-restriction per video
Live comment / like / watch-count counters with eventual consistency
nonFunctional: P99 segment fetch under 100 ms from CDN edge globally
Durability 11 nines for source and transcoded assets
Scale to 2B DAU, ~115K segment QPS sustained, ~350K peak
Transcoding pipeline elastic to 100+ concurrent encodes
Cost efficiency: origin egress under 5% of total playback bandwidth

assumptions: 2B DAU, 5 videos watched per user per day → 10B views/day
Transcoded to 6 adaptive-bitrate ladders (240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) + HLS 6s segments
Video retained forever (no expiry); metadata updates on transcode completion via completion queue
CDN hit ratio target: 95%+ for the long-tail head; origin absorbs <5% of playback QPS
estimates: Origin egress: 5% of peak = 17K segments/sec — CDN absorbs the rest
Storage: 500K * 100MB * 4x (ladders + HLS overhead) / day ≈ 200 TB/day, 73 PB/year
Transcoding: 500K uploads * avg 10 min compute / 86400 ≈ 35 concurrent encodes baseline, peak 100+

client.name: Client (Web / Mobile / TV)
client.summary: HLS/DASH player that adapts bitrate based on network and buffer; also chunks uploads into GOP-aligned pieces for parallel transfer.

sections.heading: Adaptive bitrate playback
sections.body: The player (HLS.js / ExoPlayer / AVPlayer) fetches the master playlist, picks an initial ladder from bandwidth probes, then re-ladders mid-stream based on buffer fill and measured throughput. This is the book's 'adaptive bitrate streaming' — the same video is encoded into multiple bitrates and the client switches ladders transparently.

sections.heading: Parallel chunked upload
sections.body: The book calls out three ways to speed up uploads: (1) split the source into chunks, (2) upload chunks in parallel, (3) use upload points geographically near the user. Clients split the file into ~5 MB / GOP-aligned chunks, hash each, and issue parallel PUTs. A lost chunk retries locally; the whole upload never restarts.

sections.heading: Upload points near users
sections.body: The client resolves the nearest regional upload endpoint (anycast or latency-based DNS) so the original bytes hit a close-by PoP, which then replicates into the central original-storage bucket.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The player does half the streaming work — bandwidth estimation, ladder selection, prefetch. A good player masks CDN hiccups that would otherwise be visible rebuffers. Parallel chunked uploads are what make uploading a 4 GB 4K source over home Wi-Fi actually finish without the user retrying.

bottlenecks.title: Rebuffering from stale ABR ladder selection
bottlenecks.trigger: Network throughput drops mid-playback (e.g. mobile handoff, Wi-Fi congestion) while the player is mid-6s-segment on a 1080p/4K ladder; with HLS 6s segments the player can't switch ladder until the current segment drains
bottlenecks.symptom: Visible spinner / rebuffer events, especially on mobile; viewers on 4K ladder stall for 2–6s before dropping to 720p
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune HLS.js/ExoPlayer ABR to use buffer-based algorithms (BOLA) with conservative initial ladder, keep 20–30s forward buffer, enable LL-HLS or shorter 2s segments for live-like responsiveness, and pre-fetch the next segment at the adjacent lower ladder
bottlenecks.detection: Client-side QoE beacons reporting rebuffer ratio (target <0.5%), time-to-first-frame, and ladder-switch count per session; alert when p95 rebuffer ratio exceeds 1% per region

bottlenecks.title: Parallel chunked upload exhausting client CPU / memory
bottlenecks.trigger: User uploads a 4 GB 4K source split into ~800 chunks of 5 MB each; too-high parallelism (e.g. 16+ concurrent PUTs) saturates mobile CPU on hashing and TLS, or a flaky connection triggers retry storms on every chunk
bottlenecks.symptom: Upload stalls or actually runs slower than serial; mobile device heats up, app gets OOM-killed by the OS mid-upload; 580 MB/s aggregate peak is never reached because individual clients underperform
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap concurrency at 4–6 parallel chunks, adapt dynamically to measured throughput, use streaming SHA-256 instead of buffering whole chunks, and persist per-chunk upload state to disk so app kills resume instead of restart
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry on upload goodput (MB/s), chunk retry rate, and upload abandonment rate; alert if >5% of uploads >100 MB fail to complete within 3x the theoretical time

bottlenecks.title: Watch-page cold start fanout latency
bottlenecks.trigger: Watch page load issues parallel requests: metadata via API, recommendations (50ms p99), master manifest from CDN, and first 2 segments — on a cold CDN edge (long-tail video, 60–70% hit ratio) the first segment pulls from shield → transcoded storage (10–80ms)
bottlenecks.symptom: Time-to-first-frame >2s on long-tail content; users abandon before playback starts, especially on recommendation-driven clicks into obscure videos
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client issues manifest + segment prefetch in parallel with metadata call (don't serialize), uses HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 multiplexing to a single CDN host, and requests lowest ladder first for fast startup then re-ladders up after 1–2 segments
bottlenecks.detection: Client beacon for time-to-first-frame broken down by CDN hit/miss; alert when p95 TTFF exceeds 1.5s, and correlate with CDN X-Cache header miss rate in client logs

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is a first-class component here In most systems the client is a dumb terminal — it makes requests, renders responses, done. But for a YouTube-scale video platform, the client is doing *real* engineering work on both sides of the pipe. On playback, an HLS/DASH player is constantly measuring throughput and buffer fill to decide whether to fetch the next 6-second chunk at 480p or 4K. On upload, it's splitting a 4 GB source into GOP-aligned chunks and pushing them in parallel to the nearest PoP. The design leans on the client because serving 10B views/day and absorbing 500K uploads/day is only tractable if the endpoints cooperate. ## What happens without a smart client If the player didn't do adaptive bitrate, every viewer would lock to one ladder — a mobile user on a subway would either stall forever on 1080p or watch 240p the whole train ride. If uploads weren't chunked and parallelized, a user on a 20 Mbps home connection uploading a 4 GB 4K source would hold a single TCP connection open for ~30 minutes; one packet loss near the end restarts the entire transfer, and the original-storage bucket sees a flood of retries from frustrated users. ## The number that makes this obvious Peak playback is ~350K segment requests/sec globally. The design targets a 95%+ CDN hit ratio, leaving ~17K/sec for origin. That 17K number only holds if clients intelligently back off to a lower ladder during congestion instead of hammering the CDN for a 4K segment they'll never finish in time — the client's ABR logic is literally what keeps origin load inside its budget. ## The trade-off Pushing logic into the client means you ship *and debug* three player codebases (web, mobile, TV) instead of one server-side encoder pipeline.

cdn.name: CDN Edge
cdn.summary: Geographically distributed edge caches serving HLS/DASH segments close to the viewer; falls back to transcoded-storage origin on miss.

sections.heading: Cache key
sections.body: `{video_id}/{ladder}/{segment_n}.ts` — segments are immutable once written, so TTL can be effectively infinite. Master / media playlists get short TTLs (e.g. 60s) so a new ladder added post-upload becomes visible quickly.

sections.heading: Origin fallback (the book's streaming flow)
sections.body: On a cache miss, the edge pulls from a regional shield, and the shield pulls from transcoded storage (the origin). Shielding collapses many edge misses into a single origin fetch, cutting origin QPS ~10x.

sections.heading: Hit ratio target
sections.body: 95%+ for the popular head; long-tail (old / obscure) may sit at 60–70% and benefit from pre-warming on signals (trending list promoted to shield).

sections.heading: Purge
sections.body: Rare (segments are immutable). Re-encodes write new segment names, so the old URL naturally ages out.

lost: Fewer PoPs than Cloudflare/Akamai in some regions

gained: Workers at edge for auth / per-request logic
lost: Per-GB pricing can dominate at multi-PB scale

bottlenecks.title: Origin stampede on viral cold content
bottlenecks.trigger: A newly uploaded video suddenly trends and 10K+ viewers per second hit edges that haven't cached its segments yet; without request coalescing the edges all miss simultaneously and fan out to the regional shield, which in turn fans out to transcoded storage — a single 6s segment could trigger thousands of concurrent origin GETs against the 17K segment/sec origin budget (5% of 350K peak)
bottlenecks.symptom: Transcoded-storage origin egress spikes 5–10x above the 17K/sec design target, p99 time-to-first-frame jumps to 3–5s for the viral video and collateral damage hits unrelated videos as the shield saturates; on-call sees origin 503s or throttling
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable request coalescing / collapsed forwarding at both edge and shield tier (Cloudflare Argo, CloudFront Origin Shield, Varnish request coalescing), pre-warm shields on trending-list signal from the recommendation pipeline, and set stale-while-revalidate on media playlists so a single origin fetch serves all concurrent waiters
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor origin egress QPS vs. the 17K/sec budget with a 2-min rolling alert at 80% (13.5K/sec); track per-video origin-fetch-per-edge-miss ratio (healthy is ~1.0, coalescing failure shows >5); alert on shield tier CPU >70%

bottlenecks.title: Long-tail cache churn pushing hit ratio below 95% target
bottlenecks.trigger: With 73 PB/year of transcoded content and edge SSD capacity of only tens of TB per PoP, LRU eviction constantly churns long-tail videos (old, niche, recommendation-surfaced obscure content). The design targets 95%+ hit ratio but long-tail sits at 60–70%, and if the long-tail share of traffic grows (e.g. recommendation algorithm change), overall hit ratio drops below 95%
bottlenecks.symptom: Origin QPS creeps from <5% toward 10–15% of the 350K peak (35–50K segment/sec origin load, 2–3x the 17K/sec budget), transcoded-storage egress bill spikes, p95 TTFF degrades especially in smaller regions with fewer PoPs
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a mid-tier regional shield cache with larger capacity (hundreds of TB) to absorb long-tail between edge and origin; use tiered caching with hot segments on NVMe and warm on SATA SSD at edge; shard cache keys across PoP peers (consistent hashing) so a region shares one logical long-tail cache
bottlenecks.detection: Per-region hit ratio dashboards with alerts below 93% for head content and below 65% for long-tail; track origin-to-edge bytes ratio weekly; X-Cache miss rate in client QoE beacons cross-referenced with video age

bottlenecks.title: Master/media playlist short-TTL revalidation storm
bottlenecks.trigger: Master and media playlists use 60s TTL (vs. infinite TTL on immutable segments) so that newly-added ladders become visible quickly. At 350K peak segment QPS, the implied playlist QPS is ~15–20K/sec (one playlist fetch per session + periodic refresh for live-ish content); every 60s every edge revalidates against origin, producing synchronized thundering-herd against transcoded storage
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 60-second-interval latency spikes on origin (visible as sawtooth pattern in origin QPS graph), occasional manifest fetch 5xx during revalidate windows causing player startup failures, transcoded-storage p99 latency jumps from 80ms baseline to 300ms+
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use stale-while-revalidate with jittered TTL (55–65s randomized) to de-synchronize edges; bump TTL to 5min for VOD (non-live) manifests since post-upload ladder changes are rare; push manifest invalidation via explicit purge from the completion handler instead of relying on TTL expiry
bottlenecks.detection: Graph origin QPS at 10s resolution looking for 60s-period oscillation; alert on manifest fetch error rate >0.1% at edge; track completion-handler purge success rate vs. manifest version drift in client logs

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the CDN is here for YouTube-scale streaming This system is ~99% reads: 10 billion views/day against only 500K uploads/day. Video segments are also *huge* compared to typical web payloads — a single HLS segment is a few MB, and every viewer pulls a new one every 6 seconds for the entire watch. If every playback request hit a central origin, you'd be shipping petabytes per day across the internet from a handful of data centers, and viewers in Jakarta or São Paulo would wait on round-trips to Virginia. The CDN exists because **the only affordable way to serve video at this scale is to push bytes physically close to the viewer** and cache them there. ## What happens without it Without edge caching, the transcoded-storage origin becomes the bottleneck. Viewers see multi-second buffering as segments traverse continents; the origin's egress bill explodes; and one trending video triggers a thundering herd that starves every *other* video of bandwidth. The metadata DB and API are fine — they're tiny — but the storage layer melts. ## The number that makes it obvious Peak playback is ~350K segment requests/sec. With a 95% CDN hit ratio, origin sees 350K × 5% = **17.5K req/sec**. Without the CDN, origin would eat the full 350K/sec — a 20x increase, and each request is a multi-MB segment. Transcoded storage is provisioned for ~20K concurrency; it would collapse almost immediately. ## The trade-off You accept a cache-consistency headache (stale manifests, cold-start misses on long-tail videos) and a significant CDN bill in exchange for making global video delivery physically possible.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 LB for control-plane traffic (API calls, upload initiation), NOT for segment GETs.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: Only API, upload session negotiation, and metadata calls flow through here. Segment playback goes client → CDN directly, and chunk bytes go client → original-storage via signed URLs — the LB never carries a 100 MB payload.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin across stateless API replicas; health-check ejection on 3 consecutive 5xx.

bottlenecks.title: Connection table exhaustion from upload session longevity
bottlenecks.trigger: Upload flows hold LB-fronted API connections open across signed-URL negotiation, chunk-plan coordination, and completion callbacks. With 500K uploads/day averaging 10+ minutes wall-clock and bursty regional peaks, concurrent in-flight upload sessions can push into the tens of thousands against the LB's 50K concurrency ceiling — compounded by watch-page API traffic at 115K playback QPS feeding metadata lookups through the same LB.
bottlenecks.symptom: New API connections get queued or reset with 503s; upload initiation POSTs time out intermittently; watch-page metadata calls see elevated p99 latency (>500ms) even though backend API replicas are healthy; LB CPU normal but active-connection graph pinned near ceiling.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split the LB into two pools — one for short-lived watch-page/metadata traffic, one for upload control-plane — each sized independently; set aggressive idle timeouts (15s) on the metadata pool and HTTP/2 multiplexing on the upload pool to collapse per-client connections; ensure chunk byte uploads go via signed URL direct to original-storage and never touch this LB.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on active-connection count >70% of 50K concurrency limit (35K) over 2-min window; track connection-age p99 per pool and alert if metadata-pool p99 exceeds 30s (indicates upload traffic bleeding in); monitor 503 rate at LB tier with <0.05% threshold.

bottlenecks.title: Health-check eject cascade during API deploy or GC pause
bottlenecks.trigger: LB ejects API replicas on 3 consecutive 5xx. During a rolling deploy of the stateless API fleet (or a coordinated JVM/Go GC pause across replicas under the 115K playback QPS load), multiple replicas can trip the ejection threshold within seconds, shrinking the active pool below what the 3000-concurrency-per-replica budget needs to absorb peak traffic.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden latency cliff on watch-page loads (p99 spikes from 20ms to 500ms+); upstream queue depth on remaining API replicas spikes; 503 rate at LB climbs to 1–5% for 30–60 seconds; eventually recovers as ejected replicas pass health checks and re-enter rotation.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch from round-robin to least-outstanding-requests so a slow replica naturally sheds load before hitting the 5xx threshold; add panic-mode (envoy-style) that disables outlier ejection when >30% of the pool is unhealthy; enforce max 1 replica ejected per 10s window; coordinate deploys to touch <10% of pool concurrently.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when healthy-upstream-count drops below 80% of configured pool size for >30s; track ejections-per-minute with threshold >3; correlate LB 5xx rate with API replica count in a single dashboard to catch cascade patterns early.

bottlenecks.title: TLS handshake CPU pressure from watch-page fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: Every watch-page load issues parallel API calls (metadata, recommendations, user state) that terminate TLS at the LB. At peak 115K playback QPS with 2–3 API calls per watch and cold connections from mobile clients roaming between cell towers, TLS handshake rate at the LB can approach 50K+ handshakes/sec, which is where software TLS termination starts eating CPU budget needed for request forwarding.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU climbs to 70–90% even when request-forwarding rate looks normal; p99 connection-establishment time rises from ~20ms to 100ms+; mobile clients on flaky networks see disproportionate TTFF regression; backend API replicas report low utilization (bottleneck is above them).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets with 24h rotation) and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 with connection coalescing so one client reuses one TLS session across all watch-page API calls; offload to hardware TLS (AWS NLB+ALB chain, or dedicated TLS-terminating nodes with AES-NI); enforce ECDSA certs over RSA-2048 to cut handshake CPU ~5x.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor TLS-handshakes-per-second vs. requests-per-second ratio (healthy <0.2 with resumption; >0.5 means resumption is broken); alert on LB CPU >75% sustained 5 min; track session-resumption-hit-rate with target >80%.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a load balancer is here — but *only* for the control plane In a YouTube-style system, the scary traffic is video bytes: 350K segment requests/sec at peak, plus 580 MB/s of upload throughput. None of that goes through this load balancer. Segment playback goes client → CDN directly, and source uploads go client → original storage via signed URLs. What this LB actually fronts is the small, chatty control-plane traffic: watch-page metadata calls, recommendation requests, upload session negotiation, and signed-URL issuance. You still need it because those API calls fan out from billions of users to a stateless API fleet that must be sized, deployed, and health-checked independently — and somebody has to terminate TLS and spread connections across replicas. ## What happens without it If clients pinned directly to API hosts, a single rolling deploy or crashed replica would strand millions of watch pages with 5xx errors and no failover. Operators would see connection-refused spikes; users would see "video unavailable" on load even though the CDN is happily serving segments. The metadata DB and cache wouldn't even get the chance to respond. ## The number that justifies keeping it small At 115K playback QPS, each watch page fires ~2–3 API calls (metadata + recommendations), so the LB sees roughly 300K req/sec — tiny compared to the 350K *segment* QPS it avoids. Sized at 50K concurrent connections, it handles control-plane fanout without ever carrying a 100 MB video payload. ## Trade-off You accept an extra network hop and a TLS-handshake CPU tax on API calls to get clean rolling deploys and replica-level failover.

api.name: Video API
api.summary: Metadata CRUD, upload session coordination, signed-URL issuance to original storage, and playback manifest URL lookup.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
POST /videos # create metadata (status=UPLOADING), return upload URL + chunk plan
PATCH /videos/:id # title / desc updates
GET /videos/:id # metadata + playback manifest URL (from CDN)
GET /videos/:id/recommendations
```

sections.heading: Upload flow (book's 6 steps)
sections.body:
1. Client POSTs metadata; API creates row with status=UPLOADING and returns a signed URL for original storage
2. Client uploads source (chunked + parallel) directly to original storage — not through the API
3. Original-storage event triggers a transcoding job (job metadata written to the transcoding pipeline)
4. Transcoding writes outputs to transcoded storage and to the CDN
5. A completion event lands on the completion queue
6. The completion handler updates metadata DB (status=READY, ladder list) and invalidates cache
The book explicitly shows uploading metadata and uploading video happening in parallel — this is why clients sometimes see 'processing' on the watch page before ladders are ready.

sections.heading: Signed URLs
sections.body: 15-min TTL, scoped to a single original-storage key. Prevents upload forgery without routing bytes through the API.

bottlenecks.title: Watch-page metadata fanout saturating API concurrency budget
bottlenecks.trigger: At peak 350K segment QPS with ~115K concurrent watch sessions, each watch page fires 2–3 API calls (GET /videos/:id, recommendations, user state) producing ~300K API req/sec against a fleet sized at 3000 concurrency per replica; a Redis cache miss or slight degradation drops the 95% hit ratio and pushes metadata-DB-bound calls (3–10ms service time) past the concurrency ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: API p99 latency climbs from ~15ms to 200–500ms, watch pages show blank metadata or 'loading' spinners even though CDN segments play fine; upstream LB queues grow and eventually 503s appear; on-call sees API replica CPU moderate but request queue depth pinned.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce strict cache-aside with singleflight/request coalescing so a single miss doesn't stampede metadata DB; add negative caching for non-existent/unreleased videos; set per-endpoint concurrency limits with fast-fail (Hystrix/resilience4j bulkheads) at 80% of replica budget; horizontally autoscale on request-queue-depth not CPU; pre-populate cache on video READY transition via completion handler write-through.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache hit ratio <93% for video:{id} over 2-min window; track API in-flight-requests-per-replica with threshold >2400 (80% of 3000); p99 latency SLO alert at 50ms for GET /videos/:id; correlate metadata-DB QPS against cache-miss rate to spot stampede patterns.

bottlenecks.title: Signed-URL issuance and upload session coordination blocking under upload bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day concentrate in regional prime hours (e.g. evening in each timezone), producing bursts 3–5x average. Each upload triggers POST /videos (metadata row insert + signed-URL generation + chunk plan response) plus periodic PATCH calls during the 10+ min upload; signed-URL crypto (HMAC/RSA signing) is CPU-heavy and shares the same 3000 concurrency budget as watch-page traffic.
bottlenecks.symptom: Upload initiation POSTs time out or return 503 during regional peaks; users retry, producing duplicate UPLOADING metadata rows and wasted original-storage signed URLs; watch-page latency collaterally degrades because upload CPU is crowding out metadata reads.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split the API into two deployments (read-path vs upload-path) behind separate LB pools so upload CPU spikes don't starve watch-page reads; cache signing keys in memory and batch signed-URL minting; use ECDSA over RSA-2048 for ~5x faster signing; pre-generate chunk plans deterministically from file size rather than per-request computation; idempotency keys on POST /videos to dedupe retries.
bottlenecks.detection: Track upload-initiation p99 latency with <200ms SLO; alert on duplicate UPLOADING rows per owner_id >2/min (retry signal); monitor API CPU time attributed to crypto ops via pprof/flame graphs; per-endpoint error budget dashboard splitting /videos POST vs GET.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key metadata writes on view counts and status transitions
bottlenecks.trigger: View-count updates at 115K avg / 350K peak playback QPS, if any code path accidentally routes through the API's UPDATE videos path instead of the Kafka batched stream, would overwhelm the single metadata row's lock contention. Similarly, viral-video state transitions (title edits during a trending moment) trigger cache invalidation on a key being read at tens of thousands of QPS, causing thundering-herd DB hits via the API.
bottlenecks.symptom: Metadata DB sees row-level lock waits on hot video_ids, API PATCH calls time out, cache invalidation on a trending video causes a burst of DB reads through the API that spike p99 across all videos sharing the same shard; creator sees 'save failed' on title edits during viral moments.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Strictly enforce the Kafka-based view-count path — add a lint/guard rejecting UPDATE statements on view_count from API code; use cache invalidation with stale-while-revalidate and singleflight on the API layer so only one request repopulates a hot key; shard metadata DB by video_id hash once any single primary exceeds 60% CPU; soft-TTL extensions on recently-hot keys to avoid invalidation storms.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor per-row update QPS on metadata DB with alert >100/sec on any single video_id; track cache-miss burst rate (misses/sec per key) with alert on any key exceeding 1K/sec; dashboard for DB lock-wait time with p99 SLO <5ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Video API is here The Video API is the **control plane** for YouTube-style streaming. Notice what it deliberately *doesn't* do: it never carries a video byte. The 100 MB source upload goes straight from client to original storage via a signed URL, and the 350K/sec peak segment playback goes client → CDN. What the API *does* handle is the small, chatty coordination work: creating the metadata row when an upload starts, minting those signed URLs, serving the watch page's title/description/ladder list, and telling the client where the manifest lives. Without a dedicated API layer, there's nowhere to centralize authorization ("can this user upload? is this video private?"), schema validation, or the state machine that moves a video through `UPLOADING → TRANSCODING → READY`. ## What happens without it If clients talked directly to original storage and the metadata DB, a malicious user could forge upload requests, overwrite someone else's video row, or DoS the DB with malformed queries. Operators would see corrupt metadata rows, orphaned storage keys (uploads with no DB record), and no ability to roll out a schema change without coordinating with every client app. Watch pages would fail silently when the DB schema drifts. ## The number Peak playback is ~115K segment QPS, and each watch page fires ~2–3 API calls (metadata + recommendations). That's **~300K API req/sec** — tiny compared to the 350K *segment* QPS the CDN absorbs, but still enough that the API fleet is sized for 3000 concurrent requests per replica with Redis fronting the metadata DB at a 95%+ hit ratio. ## Trade-off You accept an extra hop and a stateful deploy target in exchange for a single place to enforce auth, validation, and lifecycle rules.

meta.name: Metadata DB
meta.summary: Relational store for video metadata (title, owner, status, view count, ladder list, manifest URL).

sections.heading: Schema
sections.body:
```
TABLE videos id BIGINT PK owner_id BIGINT title TEXT status ENUM # UPLOADING | TRANSCODING | READY | FAILED source_ref TEXT # key in original storage manifest_ref TEXT # key in transcoded storage / CDN path ladders JSONB # [{name, bitrate, resolution, codec},...] created_at TIMESTAMP
TABLE views (separate, append-only)
```

sections.heading: Why Postgres (sharded)
sections.body: Relational queries (by owner, by status) are common; JSONB ladder field is flexible. Shard by `id` hash once a single primary saturates.

sections.heading: View count
sections.body: Don't UPDATE on every view — way too hot. Views stream through Kafka → periodic batched increments (eventually consistent count).

bottlenecks.title: Hot-row write contention on view counts if not batched through Kafka
bottlenecks.trigger: At 115K avg / 350K peak playback QPS, any code path that UPDATEs videos.view_count directly (instead of going through the Kafka→batched-increment pipeline) serializes on a single row lock. A single trending video receiving even 1% of global playback (~3.5K views/sec) produces thousands of row-level lock waits per second on one Postgres primary sized for 500 concurrent queries.
bottlenecks.symptom: Postgres shows row-lock wait time climbing into hundreds of ms, autovacuum falls behind on the videos table causing bloat, PATCH /videos calls time out, and cache invalidations on hot video_ids cascade into DB stampedes that bring p99 across all metadata reads to 500ms+.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Strictly enforce the Kafka-based view-count path — move view_count to a separate append-only counter table or a dedicated KV store (Redis INCR flushed to DB every 60s); add a DB trigger or CI lint rejecting direct UPDATEs on view_count from API code; use HOT updates by keeping view_count out of indexed columns; tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor to 0.02 on the videos table.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-row UPDATE QPS >100/sec on any single video_id (pg_stat_statements + row sampling); monitor pg_locks for row-level wait events with threshold >50ms p99; track table bloat ratio on videos with alert >20%.

bottlenecks.title: Single-primary write saturation from upload state transitions + edits
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day each produce 3–5 writes (UPLOADING insert, PATCH during upload, TRANSCODING transition, READY transition from completion handler, plus title/desc edits) = ~2M writes/day baseline. Regional peaks (3–5x average) plus creator-dashboard writes push a single Postgres primary past its ~500 concurrency budget, especially when the 3–10ms service time interacts with JSONB ladder field updates (full-row rewrite, TOAST churn).
bottlenecks.symptom: Primary CPU pinned at 80%+ during evening peaks, replication lag to read replicas climbs past 5s causing stale watch-page metadata after upload completion, completion handler UPDATEs queue up on the DLQ, and API PATCH p99 degrades from 10ms to 200ms+.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard videos table by hash(id) across N primaries once single-primary CPU sustains >60%; move the ladders JSONB column to a separate videos_encoding table to avoid TOAST rewrites on every status transition; use logical replication with per-shard replicas; make completion-handler UPDATE idempotent with WHERE status!= 'READY' and batch transitions in groups of 100.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on primary CPU >70% for 5 min, replication lag >2s, and write QPS per shard >5K/sec; track pg_stat_statements for top-10 write statements by total_time; dashboard for TOAST table size growth rate on videos.

bottlenecks.title: Secondary-index query cost on owner_id / status scans
bottlenecks.trigger: Creator dashboards (`WHERE owner_id =? ORDER BY created_at DESC`) and ops queries (`WHERE status = 'TRANSCODING'` for pipeline health) hit secondary indexes. With billions of video rows accumulating (500K/day × years), a popular creator with 100K videos or a status-enum query that matches millions of rows produces index scans returning MB of rows, blowing through the shared_buffers cache and causing heap I/O spikes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Creator dashboard loads take 2–5s for prolific uploaders, ops queries on status lock up a primary for seconds, buffer cache hit ratio drops below 95%, and unrelated queries slow down due to cache eviction; read replicas show sustained I/O wait.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a covering index on (owner_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (title, status, manifest_ref) so dashboards are index-only scans; route all non-critical analytical queries (status enum scans, aging reports) to a dedicated read replica or CDC-fed data warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake); partition videos table by created_at month so old data naturally ages out of hot buffer pool; enforce LIMIT 100 + keyset pagination on creator dashboards.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor pg_stat_user_indexes for scan types (seq vs index-only) with alert on seq_scan/min >10 on videos; track buffer cache hit ratio with alert <97%; slow query log threshold at 500ms with per-endpoint attribution.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Metadata DB for YouTube-style streaming The bytes of a video — the 100 MB source and the transcoded HLS segments — live in blob storage and the CDN. But somebody has to remember *facts about* each video: who owns it, what its title is, whether it's still `UPLOADING` or `READY`, which ladders (240p…4K) exist, where the manifest lives, and whether it's public or private. Those facts are small, relational (videos belong to users, have statuses, get edited), and queried in structured ways ("all videos by creator X, newest first"). That's exactly what a SQL database is good at — and exactly what S3 and a CDN are bad at. ## What happens without it If you tried to stuff metadata into blob-storage object tags or a flat key-value store, the watch page couldn't answer "does this video exist and is it ready to play?" without scanning storage. Creator dashboards ("show me my 50 most recent uploads") would be impossible. The completion handler would have nowhere to flip a video from `TRANSCODING` to `READY`, so clients would either see broken pages mid-transcode or have to poll the CDN blindly. Operators would see orphaned storage objects with no row tying them to a user. ## The number 500K uploads/day × ~3–5 writes each (insert, upload patches, transcode transitions, ready flip) ≈ **2M writes/day baseline**, plus ~300K API reads/sec at peak playback. A single Postgres primary handles the baseline fine; the design shards by `video_id` hash once one primary saturates. ## Trade-off You accept sharding complexity and the "don't UPDATE view_count here" discipline in exchange for real relational queries and transactional state transitions.

cache.name: Metadata Cache
cache.summary: Redis cache fronting the metadata DB for watch-page reads and manifest-URL lookups.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body:
- `video:{id}` → metadata row (title, ladders, manifest URL), TTL 5 min
- `uploader:{id}:recent` → recent uploads for creator dashboards
The cache is populated write-through by the completion handler once a video flips to READY.

sections.heading: Why it matters for scale
sections.body: Watch-page loads read metadata for every video in the rail (recommendations, up-next). At 115K playback QPS, even a 95% hit ratio keeps metadata DB load sane.

sections.heading: Invalidation
sections.body: Completion handler DELs the key on state transitions (UPLOADING → READY). Title / description edits also invalidate.

gained: Slightly lower latency on pure GETs

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key thundering herd on trending video invalidation
bottlenecks.trigger: A video trending at 10K+ QPS has its video:{id} key DEL'd by the completion handler on a title/description edit or status transition; with 5-min TTL expiry on a key being read tens of thousands of times per second, every concurrent reader misses simultaneously and stampedes the metadata DB (sized for only 500 concurrent queries) through the API layer
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden latency cliff on watch pages for the trending video and collateral damage to unrelated videos sharing the same DB shard; metadata DB CPU spikes to 90%+ for 5-30 seconds; API p99 jumps from 15ms to 500ms+; cache fill rate on video:{id} shows a burst of thousands of identical SET operations within a second
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement singleflight / request coalescing at the API layer so only one request per key repopulates on miss (golang/x/sync singleflight, or Redis SET NX lock); use stale-while-revalidate pattern — serve stale cached value while one request refreshes in background; jitter TTLs by ±20% to avoid synchronized expiry; on completion handler state transitions, prefer write-through (SET new value) over DEL to eliminate the miss window entirely
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-key miss burst rate >1K misses/sec on any single cache key (Redis MONITOR sampling or client-side instrumentation); track cache-miss-to-DB-query ratio with alert when it exceeds 1.2 (indicates stampede); dashboard for top-10 hottest keys by GET QPS with cross-reference to their miss rate

bottlenecks.title: Hit ratio degradation blowing through metadata DB capacity budget
bottlenecks.trigger: At 115K avg / 350K peak playback QPS with 2-3 API calls per watch page, cache sees ~300K GET/sec; the design assumes 95% hit ratio leaving ~15K/sec to metadata DB (within its 500-concurrency × 3-10ms service time budget). A Redis memory-pressure eviction event, a recommendation algorithm change surfacing more long-tail content, or a cache node failure dropping to 90% hit ratio doubles DB load to 30K/sec — 6x the DB's sustainable QPS
bottlenecks.symptom: Metadata DB connection pool exhaustion, API request queues back up, watch pages show blank metadata/loading spinners despite CDN segments playing fine; Redis memory usage graph shows eviction counter climbing; long-tail video metadata fetches take 200ms+ while popular videos remain fast
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size Redis cluster for 2x working set (billions of video metadata × ~2KB each ≈ sufficient RAM across shards); use allkeys-lru eviction with per-key TTLs to retain hot data; add a second-tier cache (local API in-process LRU, e.g. Caffeine/Ristretto) for top-1000 hottest keys to absorb spikes; negative-cache missing video_ids with 30s TTL; replicate each Redis shard (primary + 2 replicas) to survive node loss without hit-ratio drop
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on global cache hit ratio <93% over 2-min window (vs 95% design target); monitor Redis evicted_keys counter with alert on non-zero rate sustained >1 min; track metadata DB QPS with hard alert at 10K/sec (2x budget); per-Redis-shard memory usage alert at 80%

bottlenecks.title: Cross-region invalidation staleness after completion handler writes
bottlenecks.trigger: Completion handler runs in the primary region and write-throughs the video:{id} key, but Redis replicas in other regions lag by 100ms-2s on async replication; a viewer in a different region loads the watch page right after transcode completes and gets a stale UPLOADING/TRANSCODING status from their local cache, or gets the pre-edit title after a creator edit
bottlenecks.symptom: Creator edits title, sees it update in their region, but reports from viewers in other regions show old title for up to several seconds; newly-READY videos show 'processing' spinner in some regions while others play fine; support tickets about 'my video isn't appearing' immediately post-upload
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Redis pub/sub or a Kafka-based invalidation fanout so completion handler publishes invalidations to all regional cache clusters in parallel rather than relying on replication; include a monotonic version field in cached values and have API re-fetch from DB if client supplies a higher version (read-your-writes for creators); set shorter TTL (60s instead of 5min) for keys in status=TRANSCODING to bound staleness window on the critical post-upload transition
bottlenecks.detection: Track cross-region cache-vs-DB version drift by sampling (compare cached row version to authoritative DB row every N seconds); alert on p99 staleness >5s; monitor completion-handler-to-cache-warm latency per region with SLO <500ms; track support ticket rate tagged 'video not appearing' as leading indicator

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a metadata cache for a YouTube-style platform The watch page isn't just one metadata lookup — it's a fanout. Every time a user loads a video, the API needs the title, description, ladder list, and manifest URL for the *main* video, plus the same fields for every thumbnail in the "up next" rail (often 10–20 videos). Without a cache in front of the metadata DB, every click becomes 10–20 synchronous SQL reads against Postgres, and that DB is also absorbing writes from 500K uploads/day and state transitions from the completion handler. The cache exists because the watch page's read pattern is *read-heavy, repetitive, and bursty on trending content* — exactly the shape Redis eats for breakfast and Postgres chokes on. ## What happens without it A trending video getting 10K watches/sec would hammer the metadata DB's single hot row. You'd see Postgres CPU pinned, replication lag spiking, and the API returning 500s on the watch page — even though the CDN is perfectly happy serving the actual video bytes. Operators would watch an outage where *the video plays but the page won't load*. ## The number Peak playback is **~115K segment requests/sec**, and each watch page triggers 2–3 API metadata calls → roughly **300K metadata reads/sec**. At 95% cache hit ratio, the DB sees 300K × 5% = **15K reads/sec** — survivable for a sharded Postgres. Without the cache, the DB would face the full 300K/sec, which is ~20x its practical ceiling. ## Trade-off You accept staleness (title edits take up to 5 minutes to propagate, mitigated by the completion handler's write-through) in exchange for keeping the DB alive under read storms.

origstore.name: Original Storage
origstore.summary: S3-style bucket holding raw source uploads; the book's first stop for uploaded bytes before transcoding.

sections.heading: Why a separate bucket from transcoded
sections.body: The book explicitly splits original storage (raw uploads) from transcoded storage (encoded ladders). Source videos are large, written once, read once by the transcoder, and never served to end users. Keeping them in a different bucket simplifies retention and access-control.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
sections.body: Raw source retained 7–30 days post-transcode (for re-encode if a new codec rolls out), then moved to cold storage / Glacier. Some designs delete source entirely once transcoded ladders exist.

sections.heading: Kickoff
sections.body: Object-created events from original storage trigger the transcoding pipeline. This is how 'upload complete' turns into 'encode starts' without the API mediating.

gained: Cheap at PB scale on owned hardware

bottlenecks.title: Write throughput saturation from parallel chunked uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day × 100MB avg = 580 MB/s peak aggregate, but each upload is split into ~20 chunks (5MB each) with 4-6 parallel PUTs per client; regional prime-hour bursts (3-5x average) produce ~150K-250K concurrent PUT operations fanning into a single bucket, potentially exceeding S3's default 3500 PUT/s per prefix limit if video_ids aren't hashed across prefixes
bottlenecks.symptom: Upload PUTs return 503 SlowDown errors during regional peaks, clients see chunks repeatedly retrying and upload wall-clock time balloons from 5min to 30min+, failure rate climbs above the 0.1% design target, and users abandon uploads mid-transfer producing orphaned partial objects
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hash-prefix object keys (e.g. `/{hash(video_id)[:4]}/{video_id}/source.mp4`) to spread writes across thousands of S3 partitions; request S3 request-rate increase from AWS support for known peak windows; use S3 Transfer Acceleration or regional upload endpoints so clients hit the nearest PoP; enforce client-side concurrency cap of 4-6 parallel chunks per upload
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on 503 SlowDown rate >0.01% of PUT requests over 2-min window (CloudWatch S3 metrics); track p99 chunk PUT latency with SLO <500ms; dashboard for per-prefix request rate to catch hot-prefix drift; monitor incomplete multipart upload count with alert >10K

bottlenecks.title: Storage cost blowup from undeleted source retention
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day × 100MB = 50TB/day of raw source; if the 7-30 day retention lifecycle rule fails to execute or is disabled for 're-encode safety,' source accumulates at 1.5PB/month in hot standard storage tier, on top of the 73PB/year of transcoded content; a single misconfigured lifecycle rule or a pending re-encode project (new codec rollout) can pin all source in standard tier indefinitely
bottlenecks.symptom: Monthly S3 bill for original-storage bucket grows linearly without plateauing, storage cost per upload diverges from the cost model, FinOps alerts on budget overrun; during codec migrations the team is tempted to keep source hot 'just in case' and the bill doubles
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce S3 Lifecycle policy: transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval at 7 days, delete at 30 days; tag objects with `transcode_status=complete` via completion handler so lifecycle rules key on that; automate source deletion triggered by completion handler after verification that all ladders exist in transcoded storage; quarterly audit of objects in standard tier older than 7 days
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on bucket size growth rate exceeding 50TB/day baseline by >20%; dashboard for object-age distribution with alert if >5% of objects are >30 days old in standard tier; monthly cost-per-upload metric with threshold; S3 Storage Lens for lifecycle rule execution success rate

bottlenecks.title: Transcoding trigger event loss or duplication from object-created notifications
bottlenecks.trigger: Object-created events from original storage kick off the transcoding DAG; with 500K uploads/day fanning out events to SNS/EventBridge/Lambda, at-least-once delivery semantics plus multipart upload completion (a single upload produces one CompleteMultipartUpload event, but partial PUTs can confuse naive handlers) cause duplicate or missed transcode starts, especially during S3 event notification throttling windows
bottlenecks.symptom: Some uploads sit in UPLOADING status forever because the transcode kickoff event was dropped; other videos trigger 2-3 concurrent transcodes wasting GPU budget (100 concurrent encodes at peak) and producing racing writes to transcoded storage; completion handler sees duplicate READY transitions
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route S3 events through a durable queue (SQS/Kafka) with explicit deduplication by object ETag + key; only listen for `s3:ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload` not per-part events; make the transcoding job-start path idempotent via `INSERT... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on a transcode_jobs table keyed by source_ref; add a reconciliation job that scans for videos in UPLOADING state >1hr and re-triggers
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on videos stuck in UPLOADING status >30min (should be <10min end-to-end); track ratio of S3 ObjectCreated events to transcode job starts with target 1.0 (alert on drift >2%); monitor SQS DLQ depth for failed event deliveries; dashboard for duplicate transcode starts per video_id

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Original Storage exists in this design In a YouTube-style system, the raw file a creator uploads (a 100 MB — or 4 GB for 4K — source) is fundamentally different from what viewers eventually watch. Viewers never see the source; they see transcoded HLS segments at 6 different bitrate ladders. But the transcoder needs somewhere to *pull from*, and the client needs somewhere to *push to* that isn't the API server (you never want 580 MB/s of upload bytes flowing through your API fleet). Original Storage is that staging area — a dumb, cheap, massively parallel blob store that accepts chunked PUTs via signed URLs and then fires an "object created" event to kick off transcoding. ## What happens without it If uploads went straight to the transcoder, a 20-minute encode would hold the upload connection open the whole time, and any transcoder crash would force the user to re-upload 4 GB from their home Wi-Fi. If uploads went through the API, the API fleet would need terabytes of bandwidth and would block on slow mobile clients. Operators would see API replicas pinned on network I/O while real control-plane traffic (watch pages, metadata) starves. ## The number 500K uploads/day × 100 MB avg = **50 TB/day of raw source**, peaking at ~580 MB/s. Splitting each upload into ~20 chunks of 5 MB and fanning those into a prefix-hashed bucket lets S3-class storage absorb this write volume without any single component being the bottleneck — the transcoder then reads asynchronously at its own pace. ## Trade-off You pay to store bytes no end user ever sees (mitigated by a 7–30 day lifecycle policy to Glacier) in exchange for fully decoupling upload speed from the 10+ minute encode.

tcw.name: Transcoding Servers
tcw.summary: Fleet that pulls raw source from original storage and runs a DAG of transcoding tasks to produce every ladder, thumbnail, and captions set.

sections.heading: DAG-based transcoding (book's model)
sections.body:
The book models transcoding as a directed acyclic graph of tasks, not a single monolithic encode. Typical DAG:
```
inspection ──┬─> video encoding (per ladder, 240p…4K) ─┐ ├─> audio encoding (AAC / Opus) ─────────┤ ├─> thumbnail extraction ────────────────┼─> assembler ─> completion └─> watermark / DRM packaging ───────────┘
```
Each node is a separate task with its own retry and scheduling policy. This is what lets YouTube add a new output (e.g. AV1, closed-captions) as a new node without rewriting the pipeline.

sections.heading: Pipeline
sections.body:
1. Download source chunks from original storage
2. Inspection: probe codec / duration / validity
3. Fan out to per-ladder video encodes (FFmpeg NVENC for H.264/HEVC)
4. Audio + thumbnail + watermark in parallel
5. Assembler joins all outputs, writes HLS manifest + segments to transcoded storage
6. Emit completion event to the completion queue

sections.heading: Concurrency + GPUs
sections.body: GPU-backed encoders (NVENC) for 2–5x cost/throughput win on H.264/HEVC. 100 workers × 1–2 jobs each handles peak 500K/day.

sections.heading: Failure handling
sections.body: Each DAG node retries up to 3× with backoff. A permanently failed node marks the video FAILED and pages the pipeline owner. Partial results (e.g. 720p done, 4K failed) can still go live.

gained: Fully managed, no fleet to run

bottlenecks.title: GPU encoder saturation during regional upload bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day with 10-min average encode produce ~35 concurrent encodes baseline, but regional prime-hour bursts (3-5x average) and long 4K sources (20+ min encode) push concurrent encodes past 100+, exceeding the 200-concurrency fleet budget especially when each upload fans out into 6-8 per-ladder encode tasks in the DAG
bottlenecks.symptom: Transcode queue depth climbs into the thousands, end-to-end upload-to-READY latency balloons from 10min to 1-2hrs, users see 'processing' status for hours on the watch page, creator complaints about 'my video isn't ready yet' spike, GPU utilization pinned at 100% across fleet
bottlenecks.mitigation: Autoscale GPU fleet on queue-depth signal (target depth <500 jobs); use GOP-level chunk parallelism to split a single 4K encode across N workers (book's approach — cuts wall-clock 5-10x); prioritize lower ladders (240p/480p) first so partial-READY state unblocks playback while 4K finishes; reserve spot/preemptible GPU capacity for burst absorption; use NVENC H.264 over CPU x264 for 2-5x throughput
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on transcode queue depth >1000 jobs over 5-min window; track p95 end-to-end upload-to-READY latency with SLO <30min; GPU utilization dashboard per worker with alert on fleet-wide >85% sustained 10min; per-ladder encode wait-time histogram

bottlenecks.title: DAG task retry storms from transient FFmpeg / source corruption failures
bottlenecks.trigger: Each DAG node retries up to 3x on failure; at 0.5% failure rate across 6-8 ladder encodes + audio + thumbnails + watermark per video (~10 tasks), ~5% of the 500K daily uploads (25K/day) hit at least one task retry. A bad source file (corrupt header, unusual codec) or a transient FFmpeg OOM can trigger all 3 retries on every ladder simultaneously, consuming 3x the GPU budget for that video and starving the queue
bottlenecks.symptom: Fleet GPU-hours consumed diverges from healthy baseline by 20-30%, specific video_ids show up repeatedly in retry logs, some videos eventually mark FAILED after exhausting retries while others succeed on ladder 1 but fail on ladder 2 producing partial-state videos, on-call pages spike from DLQ growth
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run inspection task FIRST as DAG gate — reject corrupt/unsupported sources before fanning out to ladder encodes (saves 95% of wasted retries); use exponential backoff with jitter on retries, not immediate; circuit-break per-source after 2 failures across any ladder (likely a bad input, not transient); isolate FFmpeg processes with memory limits + seccomp to prevent one bad source crashing the worker; cache inspection results to skip re-probing on retry
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-video retry count >5 across DAG tasks; track task-failure rate per DAG node with alert >1% on any single node; FAILED video rate SLO <0.2% of daily uploads; DLQ depth alert >100 messages; flame graph of FFmpeg crashes by source codec to catch systemic input issues

bottlenecks.title: Source-download bandwidth bottleneck from original storage
bottlenecks.trigger: Each transcode job pulls the full 100MB (or 4GB for 4K) source from original storage before encoding starts; with 200 concurrent workers each pulling a ~500MB average source, fleet ingress hits 10-50 Gbps sustained. Peak regional bursts with 4K-heavy queues push toward 100 Gbps, potentially saturating VPC/cross-AZ bandwidth or hitting S3 GET rate limits (5500 GET/s per prefix) if worker fleet isn't AZ-colocated with original-storage prefix distribution
bottlenecks.symptom: Workers show high network-wait time between job pickup and first FFmpeg frame processed (should be <10s, degrades to 60s+), GPU utilization dips to 30-40% because encoders are starved waiting for bytes, transcode wall-clock time regresses 20-50% fleet-wide, S3 GetObject p99 latency climbs from 80ms to 500ms+
bottlenecks.mitigation: Co-locate transcoding fleet in same AZ/region as original-storage buckets to minimize cross-AZ egress; use S3 Transfer Acceleration or ranged GETs to parallelize source download into chunks matching GOP boundaries (enables encode-while-downloading pipelining); cache hot source files on local NVMe for retry scenarios to avoid re-download; pre-fetch the next queued job's source during current job's encode phase
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor network-wait-to-encode-time ratio per job with alert >20% (healthy <10%); track GPU utilization with alert on <60% fleet-average (indicates starvation); S3 GetObject p99 latency from transcoding fleet with SLO <150ms; per-worker network ingress bps dashboard to catch saturation

prebuild.explanation: ## Why transcoding servers exist for YouTube-style streaming A creator uploads one file — maybe a 4 GB 4K `.mov` straight off their camera. But viewers arrive on every imaginable device and network: a phone on 3G in a tunnel, a laptop on office Wi-Fi, a 4K TV on fiber. You cannot serve that one source file to all of them. The phone would burn data and stall; the TV would get a blurry stream. Transcoding servers exist to convert that single source into **6 adaptive-bitrate ladders** (240p → 4K) plus HLS segments, thumbnails, and watermarked variants, so the client-side player can pick the right ladder on the fly. This is also why transcoding is modeled as a **DAG of tasks** (inspection → per-ladder encodes → audio → thumbnails → assembler) — you can add a new output like AV1 as a new node without rewriting the pipeline. ## What happens without it If you skipped transcoding and served the raw source from the CDN, mobile viewers would rebuffer constantly, the CDN would ship 4 GB per view instead of a few hundred MB, and adaptive bitrate simply wouldn't work — there's only one bitrate. Operators would see CDN egress costs explode and viewer retention tank. The client's ABR logic (which the design relies on to keep origin load within budget) would have nothing to switch between. ## The number 500K uploads/day × ~10 min average encode ÷ 86,400 sec = **~35 concurrent encodes baseline**, with peaks of 100+. That's why the fleet is sized around 200 GPU-backed workers (NVENC for 2–5x throughput), and why uploads go through a queue rather than blocking on encode. ## Trade-off Storage balloons 3–5x (one source becomes 6–8 ladders) and uploads take 10+ minutes to become playable — accepted in exchange for smooth playback on every device.

tcstore.name: Transcoded Storage
tcstore.summary: Authoritative home of all transcoded HLS/DASH segments and manifests; acts as the CDN's origin.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: `/{video_id}/{ladder}/segment_{n}.ts` + `/{video_id}/master.m3u8` + per-ladder media playlists.

sections.heading: Tiering
sections.body: Hot (last 30d + trending) on standard storage; cold long-tail on S3 IA / Glacier Instant Retrieval. Cross-tier on view-rate signals.

sections.heading: Origin shielding
sections.body: CDN regional shields cut origin QPS roughly 10x; origin peaks at ~17K segment GETs/sec (5% of 350K).

bottlenecks.title: Origin egress spike when CDN hit ratio drops below 95% target
bottlenecks.trigger: Design budgets origin at 5% of 350K peak segment QPS = ~17K segment GETs/sec. Any event that degrades CDN hit ratio — a recommendation algorithm surfacing more long-tail videos (which sit at 60-70% hit ratio vs. 95% head target), a regional CDN shield cache flush/restart, or a viral cold video — pushes origin QPS toward 35K-50K/sec, 2-3x the 20K concurrency ceiling of transcoded storage.
bottlenecks.symptom: Transcoded-storage p99 GET latency climbs from 80ms baseline to 500ms+, S3 returns 503 SlowDown on hot prefixes, CDN edges see origin fetch timeouts causing manifest/segment fetch failures at the player, viewers in affected regions see rebuffering and time-to-first-frame >3s, S3 egress bill spikes 5-10x overnight.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable CDN regional shield (CloudFront Origin Shield / Cloudflare Argo) to collapse edge fanout ~10x before hitting origin; hash-prefix keys as `/{hash(video_id)[:4]}/{video_id}/{ladder}/seg_{n}.ts` to spread across thousands of S3 partitions beyond the 5500 GET/s per-prefix limit; enforce request coalescing at shield tier; pre-warm shields on trending-list signal from the recommendation pipeline; set stale-while-revalidate on manifests to serve one origin response to all concurrent waiters.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on origin segment QPS >13.5K/sec (80% of 17K budget) over 2-min window; per-prefix 503 SlowDown rate with threshold >0.01%; CDN hit-ratio dashboard split by head vs long-tail with alert if overall ratio <93%; S3 GetObject p99 latency SLO <150ms.

bottlenecks.title: Cold-tier retrieval latency blowing through TTFF budget on long-tail content
bottlenecks.trigger: 73 PB/year accumulation forces aggressive tiering: hot (last 30d + trending) on standard tier, long-tail on S3 IA / Glacier Instant Retrieval. When a recommendation engine surfaces a 2-year-old video, or a creator's old content goes viral, the first segment GET hits cold tier with 100-500ms retrieval latency (vs 10-80ms hot), and with 60-70% long-tail CDN hit ratio, 30-40% of long-tail segments fetch from cold.
bottlenecks.symptom: Time-to-first-frame for long-tail videos regresses to 2-5s (vs <1.5s SLO), player shows extended loading spinner on first segment, mid-playback ladder switches trigger rebuffers when the target ladder's next segment is in cold tier, disproportionate QoE degradation on recommendation-driven watch sessions into obscure content.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep master.m3u8 and media playlists + first 2 segments of every ladder permanently in standard tier (they're tiny, ~KBs, and are always the first request); use Intelligent-Tiering with monitoring disabled rather than pure Glacier for predictable latency; pre-promote videos to hot tier on trending/recommendation signal before they're surfaced to users; size regional CDN shield with hundreds of TB capacity to absorb long-tail without falling through to cold origin.
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-tier GET latency with alert on cold-tier p99 >300ms; monitor ratio of cold-tier fetches to total origin fetches with threshold >20%; TTFF beacon from client split by video age bucket (0-30d, 30d-1yr, >1yr); dashboard for tier-transition cost per day to catch runaway promotion.

bottlenecks.title: Write-side contention from transcoder assembler fanout on new uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day × 6-8 ladders × ~100-500 HLS segments per video (6s segments of avg 5-min videos) = 300M-2B PUT ops/day, peaking at 10-30K PUT/sec during regional upload bursts (3-5x average). Transcoder assembler writes all ladders' segments for a single video_id to the same prefix `/{video_id}/...`, concentrating writes on one S3 partition and risking the 3500 PUT/s per-prefix limit on burst assemblers (GOP-parallel encode produces synchronized segment writes).
bottlenecks.symptom: Assembler tasks see 503 SlowDown on PUT, transcode completion latency grows adding minutes to upload-to-READY time, some ladders partially written producing inconsistent manifest state (master.m3u8 references segments that 404 briefly), completion handler sees duplicate/retry events inflating queue depth.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard video_id prefix hash into the key path to spread writes across partitions; batch small segment PUTs via multipart uploads where possible; write manifest (master.m3u8) LAST after all segment PUTs ack'd to avoid partial-state visibility; use S3 strong read-after-write consistency guarantees and verify segment existence before emitting completion event; rate-limit assembler write concurrency per video_id to stay under per-prefix ceilings.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on PUT 503 SlowDown rate >0.05% over 5-min window; per-video assembler wall-clock time with SLO <2min after last encode completes; monitor manifest-vs-segment consistency via synthetic GET after write with alert on mismatch; dashboard for per-prefix PUT rate distribution to catch hot-prefix drift.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Transcoded Storage is here For a YouTube-style platform, the transcoding fleet produces something very different from the raw upload: **6–8 adaptive-bitrate ladders** (240p → 4K) split into 6-second HLS segments, plus thumbnails and manifests. That output needs a permanent, authoritative home somewhere, because the CDN is a *cache*, not a source of truth — edges evict long-tail content to make room for trending videos. Transcoded Storage is the bucket the CDN falls back to on a miss, and it's what the transcoder writes to when a job finishes. Keeping it separate from Original Storage (the raw source bucket) lets each bucket have its own lifecycle: sources age out to Glacier in 30 days, but transcoded segments are kept forever because they're what viewers actually watch. ## What happens without it If transcoded outputs had nowhere durable to land, a CDN cache eviction would mean the video is *gone* — the client would get a 404 on a 2-year-old video nobody watched last month. Operators would either have to re-transcode on demand (minutes of latency, GPU cost per playback) or pin everything in the CDN forever (economically impossible). Viewers would see "video unavailable" on anything outside the trending window. ## The number The design accumulates **~200 TB/day, 73 PB/year** of transcoded output (500K uploads × 100 MB × 4x ladder overhead). At that scale, the CDN physically cannot hold everything — edge SSDs are tens of TB per PoP. Transcoded Storage absorbs the full 73 PB; the CDN caches only the hot working set, hitting the origin for the ~5% miss rate (~17K segment GETs/sec at peak). ## Trade-off You pay for petabyte-scale blob storage forever in exchange for never having to re-encode a video.

compq.name: Completion Queue
compq.summary: Durable queue of transcode-completion events produced by the transcoding DAG's assembler and drained by the completion handler.

sections.heading: Why a queue here
sections.body: Transcoding is asynchronous and variable (30s for a 1-min clip, 20+ min for a 4K hour-long). Decoupling 'encode finished' from 'metadata updated' via a durable queue means a downstream failure in the completion handler doesn't lose the fact that ladders are ready.

sections.heading: Message shape
Partitioning
sections.body: Kafka; partition by `video_id`. Strict per-video ordering — a retry must not overtake a later completion for the same id.

bottlenecks.title: Per-partition ordering bottleneck on hot video_id keys blocking throughput
bottlenecks.trigger: Kafka partitioning by video_id enforces strict per-video ordering, but retries from the transcoding DAG (each node retries up to 3x at 0.5% failure rate) can produce 3-5 completion-like events for the same video_id. With 500K uploads/day producing ~6 events per completed video (assembler + partial-ladder-ready signals + retries) = ~3M events/day, bursty regional upload peaks (3-5x average) push ~170 events/sec, and a single hot partition handling retries for a stuck viral-upload video_id serializes behind slow DB updates in the completion handler.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-partition consumer lag climbs into the thousands on specific partitions while others drain fine; end-to-end upload-to-READY latency for affected videos balloons from seconds to minutes; creators see 'processing' state linger even though transcode actually finished; on-call sees uneven partition lag distribution in Kafka dashboards.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use compacted topic semantics keyed by video_id so retry events collapse to the latest state instead of queueing serially; size partitions for 10x baseline throughput (e.g. 200 partitions for 500K uploads/day) so any single video's events are isolated; emit a single terminal completion event from the assembler instead of per-ladder events; add a secondary 'fast-path' topic for idempotent READY flips that bypasses ordering when status is already terminal.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-partition lag >500 messages over 2-min window (vs. topic-wide lag); track skew ratio (max partition lag / avg partition lag) with alert >10; dashboard for top-N hot partitions by message rate to catch video_id hotspots; monitor duplicate completion events per video_id with alert >3.

bottlenecks.title: DLQ accumulation from completion handler downstream failures
bottlenecks.trigger: Completion handler performs metadata DB UPDATE + cache write-through + downstream event fanout (search indexing, subscriber notifications, CDN pre-warm). With handler failure rate 0.1% and 500K completion events/day, baseline ~500 failed events/day land on DLQ; during metadata DB incidents (hot-row contention, replication lag >2s) or cache cluster failovers, failure rate spikes to 5-10% producing 25K-50K DLQ messages in hours, exceeding Kafka's default retention (7d) risk if not drained.
bottlenecks.symptom: DLQ depth graph climbs without plateauing, some videos stuck in TRANSCODING state for hours despite encode actually completing, manual reconciliation tickets from creators spike, on-call pages on DLQ threshold, risk of message loss if DLQ retention expires before drain.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure 30-day DLQ retention (vs. 7-day main topic) for forensic replay headroom; build an automated DLQ reprocessor that replays messages after dependency recovery with exponential backoff; split handler responsibilities — make DB UPDATE synchronous/critical and fanout events (search, notifications) async via separate downstream topics so a notification service outage doesn't DLQ the READY transition; add idempotency via WHERE status!= 'READY' so replay is safe.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on DLQ depth >100 messages over 10-min window with escalation at >1000; track DLQ-arrival-rate with alert on >10/min sustained; dashboard for time-since-oldest-DLQ-message with threshold <24hr; correlate DLQ spikes with metadata DB and cache health metrics.

bottlenecks.title: Message payload bloat from ladder/thumbnail metadata inflating broker throughput
bottlenecks.trigger: Completion event payload includes video_id, manifest_ref, ladders array (6-8 entries with codec/bitrate/resolution each), thumbnails list (typically 3-5 URLs), duration, codec_set, and timestamps — easily 2-5KB per message. At 500K/day baseline plus retries (~3M events/day) and regional peaks of 170+ events/sec, broker throughput hits 500KB-1MB/sec with bursts to 5MB/sec, which is minor in absolute terms but compounds with per-partition replication (3x replication factor) and cross-AZ network cost.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka broker disk usage grows faster than upload volume suggests, cross-AZ replication bandwidth bill creeps up, consumer fetch latency increases as message batches get larger, occasional broker GC pauses correlate with large-payload bursts during regional upload peaks.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Slim completion event payload to just {video_id, status, assembler_version} and have completion handler fetch full ladder/thumbnail metadata from a side store (transcoded storage object listing or a dedicated transcode_results table) on consume; enable Kafka broker-side compression (lz4 or zstd) to cut payload size 3-5x; set max.message.bytes conservatively (16KB) to prevent runaway payloads; use Avro/Protobuf schema registry instead of JSON for 2-3x wire savings.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor per-topic bytes-in-per-sec vs messages-in-per-sec to track average message size with alert >3KB; broker disk growth rate alert if exceeds 2x message count growth; cross-AZ replication bandwidth dashboard with monthly budget threshold; consumer fetch latency p99 SLO <50ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Completion Queue sits between transcoding and metadata For a YouTube-style platform, transcoding is wildly variable — a 1-minute clip finishes in 30 seconds, a 4K hour-long source takes 20+ minutes. When the assembler finally says "all 6–8 ladders are ready," *something* has to flip the video's metadata row from `TRANSCODING` to `READY`, warm the cache so the watch page works, kick off search indexing, and notify subscribers. You don't want the GPU-heavy transcoder doing that work directly — it's a totally different concern (database writes, cache invalidation, fanout), and if the metadata DB is briefly slow, you do *not* want a GPU worker sitting idle holding a DB connection. The queue decouples "encode finished" (a durable fact) from "everything downstream got updated" (a best-effort process that can retry). ## What happens without it If the transcoder called the metadata DB directly and the DB was down for 30 seconds, the `READY` transition would be *lost* — the encode succeeded, the segments are sitting in transcoded storage, but the watch page shows "processing" forever. Operators would see ghost videos: files exist on disk, no DB row says they're playable. Creators file tickets; on-call manually reconciles. ## The number 500K uploads/day produce completion events, but with DAG retries (each of ~10 tasks retries up to 3× at 0.5% failure) it's closer to **~3M events/day**, bursting to 170+ events/sec during regional peaks. Kafka partitioned by `video_id` absorbs this easily while guaranteeing a retry never overtakes a later completion for the same video. ## Trade-off You accept eventual consistency on the `READY` flip (seconds of delay) in exchange for never losing a completion when downstream services hiccup.

comph.name: Completion Handler
comph.summary: Consumer of the completion queue that finalizes the upload: flips metadata to READY, stores the manifest/ladder list, and warms the cache.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
1. Consume completion event
2. UPDATE videos SET status='READY', manifest_ref=..., ladders=... WHERE id =?
3. Invalidate / write-through the `video:{id}` cache key so the watch page sees ready state
4. Produce downstream events: search indexing, notifications to subscribers, CDN pre-warm on trending signal

sections.heading: Why it's a separate service
sections.body: Keeps the transcoder DAG focused on encoding; separates authorization / DB concerns from the GPU fleet. A bug in the handler (e.g. bad SQL) is isolated — it can be redeployed without restarting encodes.

sections.heading: Failure handling
sections.body: At-least-once; the DB update is idempotent (WHERE status!= 'READY'). Cache write is best-effort. Persistent failures land on a DLQ and page the video-platform oncall.

bottlenecks.title: Metadata DB write contention during regional upload bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: 500K uploads/day produce ~500K READY transitions + fanout writes, bursting 3-5x in regional prime hours (~30-50 completions/sec sustained, 100+/sec peak). Each completion does an UPDATE on videos (JSONB ladders rewrite = TOAST churn) against a metadata DB sized for 500 concurrent queries already absorbing ~15K reads/sec from watch-page traffic and ~2M writes/day from upload state transitions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Completion handler lag grows on the Kafka consumer, videos stay in TRANSCODING state for minutes despite transcode finishing; metadata DB primary CPU spikes to 80%+ during upload peaks; PATCH /videos from creators times out as handler writes crowd out API writes; downstream cache warm + search index events pile up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch completion UPDATEs in groups of 50-100 per DB transaction with idempotent `WHERE status!= 'READY'` clause; move ladders JSONB to a separate videos_encoding table to avoid TOAST rewrite on status flip; scale handler consumer fleet on Kafka lag signal (target <30s); shard metadata writes by video_id hash once single-primary write QPS exceeds 5K/sec; decouple non-critical fanout (search indexing, subscriber notifications) into downstream topics so DB commit doesn't block on them.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Kafka consumer lag for completion topic >1000 messages over 2-min window; p99 handler processing time SLO <500ms per event; track metadata DB write QPS attributed to handler with threshold >3K/sec; dashboard for upload-to-READY end-to-end latency with alert on p95 >5min.

bottlenecks.title: Cache write-through failures producing stale TRANSCODING state on watch pages
bottlenecks.trigger: Handler must DEL or SET the `video:{id}` Redis key after DB UPDATE so watch pages reflect READY state; with Redis cluster at 10K concurrency serving 300K reads/sec, any transient Redis failover, cross-region replication lag (100ms-2s), or network partition during the handler's cache call leaves the DB at READY but cache holding stale TRANSCODING status for up to 5-min TTL.
bottlenecks.symptom: Newly-completed videos show 'processing' spinner on watch page for minutes after transcode actually finished; creators refresh repeatedly and see inconsistent state across regions; support tickets spike immediately after upload completion bursts; CDN has segments ready but API says not ready yet.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use write-through (SET new value) instead of DEL to avoid the miss window entirely; publish invalidations via Redis pub/sub or a dedicated Kafka invalidation topic fanned out to all regional cache clusters in parallel rather than relying on replication; retry cache writes with exponential backoff up to 3x before logging to a reconciliation queue; short-TTL (60s) override on recently-transitioned videos to bound staleness; include monotonic version field in cached value for read-your-writes consistency.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on cache-write failure rate >0.1% of handler events; track DB-to-cache consistency drift by sampling (compare DB status vs cached status every N seconds) with alert on p99 drift >30s; monitor handler's cache-call p99 latency with SLO <10ms; dashboard for regional cache version lag post-completion.

bottlenecks.title: DLQ accumulation from downstream fanout failures during dependency incidents
bottlenecks.trigger: Handler failure rate 0.1% baseline × 500K events/day = ~500 DLQ messages/day; during metadata DB hot-row contention, replication lag >2s, or a cache cluster failover, failure rate spikes to 5-10% producing 25K-50K DLQ messages in hours. Kafka default 7d retention risks message loss if DLQ isn't drained, and fanout to search indexing + subscriber notifications + CDN pre-warm compounds failure surface area per event.
bottlenecks.symptom: DLQ depth graph climbs without plateauing, videos stuck in TRANSCODING status for hours requiring manual reconciliation, on-call paged on DLQ threshold, creator tickets about 'my video never became ready', risk of permanent message loss if retention expires before drain.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure 30-day DLQ retention (vs 7-day main topic) for forensic replay headroom; build automated DLQ reprocessor with exponential backoff triggered on dependency health recovery; split handler into critical path (DB UPDATE + cache) vs async fanout (search, notifications, CDN pre-warm) via separate downstream topics so a notification service outage doesn't DLQ the READY transition; add a reconciliation job that scans videos stuck in TRANSCODING >1hr and replays completion events from tcstore object existence.
