bottlenecks.detection: Alert on DLQ depth >100 messages over 10-min window with escalation at >1000; DLQ-arrival-rate alert >10/min sustained; track time-since-oldest-DLQ-message with threshold <24hr; correlate DLQ spikes with metadata DB and cache health dashboards; weekly audit of videos in non-terminal states >6hr old.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Completion Handler exists in this design For a YouTube-style platform, encoding a video isn't the end of the upload journey — it's the middle. Once the transcoder finishes producing 6–8 ladders and writes segments to transcoded storage, *something* still has to flip the video's metadata row from `TRANSCODING` to `READY`, warm the Redis cache so the watch page stops showing a spinner, and trigger downstream work like search indexing and subscriber notifications. You could stuff this logic into the transcoding servers, but then a GPU worker would be holding open DB connections and blocking on cache writes — wasting the most expensive fleet in the system on cheap bookkeeping. The Completion Handler is the small, boring service that does this finalization work so the GPU fleet stays focused on encoding. ## What happens without it If the transcoder wrote directly to the metadata DB and the DB was briefly slow or failing over, the `READY` transition could be *lost*. The encoded segments exist on disk, the CDN could serve them, but the watch page reads `status=TRANSCODING` forever. Creators file tickets, on-call engineers manually reconcile orphaned videos against storage, and the signal "encode succeeded" silently evaporates. ## The number 500K uploads/day, but with DAG retries (~10 tasks × up to 3 retries at 0.5% failure rate), the completion queue sees roughly **3M events/day**, bursting to 170+ events/sec in regional peaks. The handler fleet (concurrency 500) drains this easily while the transcoder fleet (concurrency 200, GPU-bound) never wastes a cycle on DB writes. ## Trade-off You accept an extra hop and seconds of delay on the `READY` flip in exchange for isolating DB/cache failures from the GPU pipeline.

rec.name: Recommendation Service
rec.summary: Returns 'up next' list for watch pages.

sections.heading: Scope in this design
sections.body: Models the call; the actual ML pipeline (candidate generation + ranking, trained offline) is a separate system.

sections.heading: Latency budget
sections.body: 50ms p99 — rec is on the critical path of the watch page but not of playback itself.

bottlenecks.title: Watch-page fanout saturating recommendation concurrency budget
bottlenecks.trigger: Every watch-page load calls GET /videos/:id/recommendations in parallel with metadata; at peak 115K playback QPS with ~1.5 rec calls per session (initial load + 'up next' refresh on video end) this produces ~170K rec req/sec against a fleet sized at 2000 concurrency per replica. With 10-50ms service time, a replica saturates at ~40-200 req/sec, requiring ~1000-4000 replicas; any ranking-model latency regression (e.g. a new embedding lookup adding 20ms) halves effective capacity overnight.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rec service p99 blows past the 50ms budget into 200-500ms, watch pages load with metadata but empty 'up next' rail, client-side timeouts trip and users see fallback static recommendations; API replicas block waiting on rec calls, bleeding latency into the metadata path even though metadata itself is healthy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce a hard 50ms deadline on the rec call from the API with circuit-breaker fallback to a cached generic 'trending in region' list; cache per-(user_id, video_id) rec results in Redis with 5-min TTL to absorb repeat views and back-button traffic; pre-compute top-N candidates offline and serve from a KV store (Bigtable/DynamoDB) for the 99% case, reserving live ranking for logged-in power users; autoscale on request-queue-depth not CPU.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on rec p99 >75ms over 2-min window (50% over budget); track in-flight-requests-per-replica with threshold >1600 (80% of 2000 concurrency); circuit-breaker trip rate dashboard with alert >0.5% of requests; watch-page 'empty rail' fallback rate as end-user QoE signal with alert >1%.

bottlenecks.title: Cold-start recommendation latency on long-tail or logged-out traffic
bottlenecks.trigger: Logged-out viewers, new users with no watch history, and watch pages for obscure long-tail videos (same traffic that drives CDN hit ratio from 95% to 60-70%) cannot use personalized pre-computed candidate lists and must fall through to live candidate generation + ranking. At 10B views/day with an estimated 10-20% logged-out or cold-start share, that's 1-2B cold rec calls/day (~13-25K QPS) hitting the slowest code path with 10-50ms service time.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rec p99 bimodal distribution: logged-in users see 15ms, cold-start users see 100ms+; time-to-first-frame for recommendation-driven clicks into obscure videos regresses because the watch page blocks on slow rec fetch; disproportionate latency degradation in regions with higher logged-out share (mobile web, embeds).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-compute a small set of contextual candidate lists keyed by coarse signals (region, language, device, current-video-id) and serve those for cold-start instead of live ranking; ship a static fallback 'trending in country' list to the client bundle so rec failures never block page render; distinguish cold vs warm paths at the LB so cold-path replicas can be sized/scaled independently.
bottlenecks.detection: Split rec latency dashboards by user_state (logged-in / logged-out / cold-start) with per-bucket p99 SLO; alert on cold-path p99 >100ms; track cold-path share of total rec QPS with alert on drift >25% (indicates logged-out traffic spike or personalization pipeline failure).

bottlenecks.title: Stale or missing candidate pools for newly-uploaded trending videos
bottlenecks.trigger: Newly-uploaded videos (500K/day, ~6/sec baseline, 20+/sec regional peaks) aren't in the offline-trained candidate generation index until the next ML pipeline run (typically hourly or daily). A video going viral within minutes of upload — common for news, sports, reactions — cannot be recommended even as it accumulates thousands of views/sec, suppressing the feedback loop that would normally amplify it.
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending videos stuck at their organic-discovery view rate while similar-vintage content from indexed creators dominates recommendations; creator complaints that 'my video is trending but not being recommended'; viral moments underperform vs. competitor platforms with faster candidate refresh; watch-time-per-session metric dips during major news events.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a real-time candidate injection path fed by the completion handler's downstream fanout — when a video flips to READY, insert it into a 'fresh candidates' pool in Redis/Bigtable keyed by creator, topic tags, and region; ranker merges fresh pool (last 24h) with offline candidates at query time with freshness-boost; run lightweight incremental index updates every 5-15 min instead of hourly; backfill view-count signal from the Kafka view-count stream with <1min lag.
bottlenecks.detection: Track median age of recommended videos with alert if >48hr (indicates index staleness); measure 'fresh candidate inclusion rate' — % of watch sessions whose rail includes a <24hr-old video — with alert if <5%; correlate trending-list membership with recommendation impression share, flag videos with high view growth but low rec impressions.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Recommendation Service for YouTube-style streaming YouTube's business model depends on viewers watching *the next* video, not just the one they clicked. The capacity estimates say 2B DAU × 5 videos/day = 10B views/day — that "5 videos per user" number only happens if something intelligently suggests what to play next when the current video ends. Without recommendations, session length collapses to 1 video per click-through from search or a shared link, and the entire economics of a CDN provisioned for 350K segment QPS stops making sense. The rec service is the component that turns a one-off playback into a session. ## What happens without it The watch page still loads — metadata comes from the cache, segments stream from the CDN — but the "up next" rail is empty. Viewers finish a video and leave. Operators see watch-time-per-session crater, ad impressions halve, and the expensively-provisioned transcoding pipeline (100+ concurrent encodes) is producing content nobody discovers. The metadata DB and CDN are fine; the *product* is broken. ## The number At peak 115K playback QPS, each watch page fires ~2–3 API calls in parallel — metadata plus recommendations. That's roughly **115K rec calls/sec** on the critical path of page load. The 50ms p99 budget exists because rec sits in parallel with the metadata fetch: if it slips past 50ms it becomes the bottleneck for *every* watch page, even though playback itself (CDN segments) is unaffected. ## Trade-off The designer accepts a whole separate ML pipeline (offline training, candidate generation, ranking) as an operational burden in exchange for the session-extension that justifies the entire platform's scale.

operations.title: Play a video (hot segment — CDN hit)
operations.name: Play a video (hot segment — CDN hit)
operations.description: Client pulls manifest + segments from CDN; origin never touched for popular content. This is the streaming flow's happy path.

steps.title: Player requests master manifest + first segment
steps.action: User hits play on video_id=vid_7a3f91. HLS.js resolves the CDN hostname via latency-based DNS, opens HTTP/2 to the nearest edge PoP, and requests master.m3u8 followed by the first segment of the starting ladder (480p for conservative startup).
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8 HTTP/2
Host: cdn.video.example
Accept: application/vnd.apple.mpegurl # then, after parsing:
GET /vid_7a3f91/480p/seg_00001.ts HTTP/2
Host: cdn.video.example
Range: bytes=0-
steps.note: Watch-page metadata is a separate flow; the player only needs the manifest URL to begin streaming.

steps.title: Edge serves manifest + segment from disk (cache HIT)
steps.action: The edge PoP has both objects cached on NVMe from earlier viewers in the region. It returns the master playlist (tiny, ~2KB) and the requested 6-second.ts segment (~3.5MB at 480p) directly, without any origin fetch. X-Cache: HIT is stamped on the response.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# conceptual edge lookup (Varnish/ATS style)
for key in ("vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8", "vid_7a3f91/480p/seg_00001.ts"): obj = cache.lookup(key) if obj and not obj.expired: respond(200, obj.body, headers={"X-Cache": "HIT", "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"}) # master.m3u8 body
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:6
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=426x240,CODECS="avc1.42e01e,mp4a.40.2"
240p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1200000,RESOLUTION=854x480,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3000000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=6000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
1080p/index.m3u8
steps.decision: HIT — origin not contacted. Subsequent segments (seg_00002, seg_00003,...) follow the same hot path.
steps.note: 95%+ of playback QPS terminates here. Transcoded-storage origin sees <5% of the 350K peak segment/sec.

steps.title: Player decodes, renders, and prefetches next segments
steps.action: HLS.js appends the.ts segment to the MediaSource buffer. Playback starts within ~400–800ms (time-to-first-frame). ABR measures observed throughput (e.g. 8 Mbps) and re-ladders up to 720p for seg_00002; it holds a 20–30s forward buffer and prefetches 2 segments ahead.
steps.codeOrCommand:
// HLS.js ABR loop
abr.observe({throughput_bps: 8_000_000, buffer_sec: 6})
next_ladder = abr.select // → "720p"
player.prefetch([ `/vid_7a3f91/${next_ladder}/seg_00002.ts`, `/vid_7a3f91/${next_ladder}/seg_00003.ts`
])
mediaSource.appendBuffer(seg_00001_bytes)
video.play
steps.note: Hot-path end-to-end TTFF is typically 300–800ms globally. Every subsequent segment GET repeats this CDN-hit loop until playback ends.

operations.title: Play a video (cold segment — CDN miss with fallback to transcoded storage)
operations.name: Play a video (cold segment — CDN miss with fallback to transcoded storage)
operations.description: First viewer in the region (long-tail or newly-promoted video): the edge misses, shield pulls from transcoded storage, segment is written into edge cache for subsequent viewers.

steps.title: Player requests first segment of a long-tail video
steps.action: User clicks a 2-year-old video (video_id=vid_a812fe) surfaced by recommendations. Player opens HTTP/2 to the nearest edge and requests the master manifest + first 240p segment (conservative startup ladder for unknown content).
steps.note: Long-tail videos sit at 60–70% CDN hit ratio vs. 95% head. Expect a miss.

steps.title: Edge MISS → regional shield MISS → origin fetch
steps.action: Edge PoP sfo-edge-14 has no entry for seg_00001 of this video. It forwards to the regional shield (sfo-shield-02); shield also misses. Request coalescing collapses any concurrent misses for the same key into one origin fetch; shield issues a single ranged GET to transcoded storage.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# edge lookup
obj = cache.lookup("vid_a812fe/240p/seg_00001.ts")
if obj is None: obj = shield.fetch(key) # request-coalesced per key # shield → origin
GET /vid_a812fe/240p/seg_00001.ts HTTP/1.1
Host: tcstore-origin.internal
Range: bytes=0-
X-Amz-Request-Id: req_coalesce_5f1e
steps.decision: MISS at edge AND shield — fall through to transcoded-storage origin

steps.title: Transcoded storage returns the segment bytes
steps.action: S3-class origin reads the segment from the backing store (standard tier for hot, IA for cold — this 2-year-old video is on IA with ~100ms retrieval latency). Returns ~1.8MB (240p is low-bitrate) with strong read-after-write consistency.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /tcstore-prod/vid_a812fe/240p/seg_00001.ts
# Object metadata
StorageClass: STANDARD_IA
ContentLength: 1887436
ETag: "b1c7e9..."
LastModified: 2024-03-14T08:12:03Z
steps.note: Origin is provisioned for ~17K segment GETs/sec (5% of 350K peak). Long-tail misses erode that budget fast if hit ratio drops.

steps.title: Shield + edge populate cache, fan out to coalesced waiters
steps.action: Shield writes the segment into its tier-2 cache (long TTL), forwards to edge PoP which writes to its NVMe tier, then streams the bytes to all coalesced waiters simultaneously. Cache-Control on the response uses stale-while-revalidate so subsequent requests skip the origin round-trip.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# shield write
shield.cache.put(key, body, ttl=2592000) # 30d # edge write + fanout
edge.cache.put(key, body, ttl=86400) # 24h (shorter; LRU churn)
for waiter in coalesced_waiters: waiter.respond(200, body, headers={ "X-Cache": "MISS, HIT (populated)", "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable, stale-while-revalidate=60" })
steps.note: Next viewer in this region gets a HIT for this segment. Cache-fill amortizes the origin cost across thousands of subsequent viewers.

steps.title: Player plays first segment, re-ladders based on observed throughput
steps.action: Total time-to-first-frame for this cold path is ~1.5–2.5s (origin retrieval + edge populate + transit) vs. ~400–800ms on the hot path. Once playing, subsequent segments will be HITs and behave like the hot path.
steps.note: Cold-path TTFF is 3–4x the hot path. Pre-warming shields on trending signal from the recommendation pipeline is the book's mitigation.

operations.title: Load watch page metadata
operations.name: Load watch page metadata
operations.description: Client fetches video metadata + recommendations. Metadata is Redis-cached after the completion handler warms it on READY transition; rec fans out in parallel.

steps.title: Client loads watch page, fires parallel API calls
steps.action: User navigates to /watch?v=vid_7a3f91. The client app issues two parallel API calls: GET /videos/:id for metadata and GET /videos/:id/recommendations for the up-next rail. Segment fetches (separate CDN flow) start in parallel the moment the manifest URL is known.
steps.note: Parallel fanout means watch-page TTFP is bounded by max(metadata, rec) not their sum.

steps.title: LB terminates TLS, round-robins to a read-path API replica
steps.action: L7 load balancer on the metadata pool (separate from the upload pool) terminates TLS with session resumption, picks api-read-23 (least outstanding requests), and forwards the plaintext request with X-Forwarded-For headers attached.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.metadata.pick(algo="least_request", healthy_only=True)
forward(req → upstream, headers.add("X-Forwarded-For", client_ip))

steps.title: API checks Redis cache (cache-aside with singleflight)
steps.action: Handler for GET /videos/:id extracts video_id, wraps a singleflight call around the Redis GET so concurrent misses for the same key don't stampede the DB, and issues the cache lookup.

steps.title: Redis returns metadata (HIT) — or MISS, fall through to DB
steps.action: 95% of the time the key is present (write-through from the completion handler on READY transition). Redis returns the serialized row in <1ms. On MISS, API falls through to the metadata DB in the next step.
steps.codeOrCommand: GET video:vid_7a3f91
steps.decision: HIT — skip the DB query in the next step. On MISS (~5%), API issues a SELECT and write-throughs the result back to cache with 5min TTL.

steps.title: Postgres SELECT (only on cache MISS)
steps.action: On the 5% miss path the API issues a primary-key lookup. Point-read on (id) hits the covering index, returns in 3–10ms. On the 95% HIT path this step is skipped entirely — shown here for completeness of the read pattern.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT id, owner_id, title, status, manifest_ref, ladders, duration_sec, created_at
FROM videos
WHERE id = 'vid_7a3f91'
LIMIT 1;
steps.note: On MISS, API also fires an async SET into Redis (write-through) so the next request is a HIT. 5% × 300K rps = 15K DB QPS — within the sharded Postgres budget.

steps.title: Recommendation service returns up-next list (in parallel)
steps.action: Fires concurrently with the metadata call — NOT sequentially. Ranker merges pre-computed candidate pool (offline-trained) with a fresh-pool injection (last 24h uploads tagged by topic) and returns top-20. Hard 50ms deadline; on timeout, API falls back to a cached 'trending in region' list so the rail never blocks page render.
steps.codeOrCommand:
ctx = deadline(50ms)
candidates = kv.get(f"cand:{user_id}") or kv.get(f"cand:region:us-west")
fresh = kv.get("fresh_pool:us-west") # <24h uploads
ranked = ranker.score(candidates + fresh, seed_video="vid_7a3f91")
return ranked[:20]

steps.title: API assembles watch-page response
steps.action: API joins the metadata row and the recommendation list into a single JSON response. Attaches the CDN manifest URL so the player can start the segment flow immediately.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return 200, { "video": { "id": "vid_7a3f91", "title": "Distributed Systems Patterns", "duration_sec": 842, "manifest": "https://cdn.video.example/vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8", "ladders": ["240p", "480p", "720p", "1080p"], "owner": {"id": "usr_creator_11", "name": "creator"}, "view_count": 1249311 }, "recommendations": [... 20 items... ]
}

steps.title: LB relays response
steps.action: Return path through the metadata LB pool. TLS session reused; no new handshake.

steps.title: Client renders watch page, triggers CDN segment flow
steps.action: Client renders title, description, creator, view count, and the 20-item up-next rail. The manifest URL from the response is handed to HLS.js which immediately begins the play flow (separate operation). Total watch-page latency: typically 30–80ms globally.
steps.codeOrCommand:
renderPage(response.video, response.recommendations)
hlsPlayer.loadSource(response.video.manifest)
hlsPlayer.attachMedia(videoElement)

operations.title: Upload a new video (metadata + parallel chunked source upload)
operations.name: Upload a new video (metadata + parallel chunked source upload)
operations.description: Per the book: client POSTs metadata AND streams source chunks in parallel. API issues a signed URL, client PUTs chunks direct to original storage, origin-bucket event triggers transcoding pipeline asynchronously, completion handler eventually flips metadata to READY.

steps.title: Client POSTs video metadata to initiate upload
steps.action: Creator selects file source.mov (312MB, H.264/AAC, 14min 02s). Client probes the file with a local inspector, computes SHA-256 of the first 1MB for dedup check, and POSTs metadata to request an upload session.
steps.note: Idempotency key dedupes retries so network flakiness doesn't create duplicate UPLOADING rows.

steps.title: LB routes to upload-path API pool
steps.action: Dedicated upload pool (separate from watch-page pool) so signed-URL crypto spikes don't starve metadata reads. HTTP/2 to the chosen API replica.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.upload.pick(algo="least_request")
forward(req → upstream)

steps.title: API authenticates, reserves video_id, mints signed multipart-upload URL
steps.action: API validates JWT, checks the creator's quota, generates a new video_id (Snowflake-style), writes a metadata row with status=UPLOADING, and initiates an S3 multipart upload against the original-storage bucket. Returns the uploadId + a chunk plan (size-based, 5MB chunks).
steps.codeOrCommand:
# auth + quota
user = jwt.verify(req.auth)
if not quota.check(user.id): return 429 # idempotent video_id
existing = db.lookup_by_idempotency_key("upl_req_9c2f")
video_id = existing or idgen.next # e.g. "vid_7a3f91" # metadata row (status=UPLOADING)
db.exec(""" INSERT INTO videos (id, owner_id, title, status, source_ref, created_at) VALUES (?,?,?, 'UPLOADING',?, NOW) ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING
""", video_id, user.id, title, f"s3://origstore-prod/{hash(video_id)[:4]}/{video_id}/source.mov") # S3 multipart init
resp = s3.create_multipart_upload( Bucket="origstore-prod", Key=f"{hash(video_id)[:4]}/{video_id}/source.mov"
)
upload_id = resp["UploadId"] # e.g. "mpu_VXBsb2FkSWQ" # chunk plan: 5MB chunks → 63 parts for 312MB source
chunks = [{"partNumber": n, "size": 5_242_880} for n in range(1, 64)] # per-part signed URLs (15-min TTL)
signed_urls = [ s3.generate_presigned_url("upload_part", Params={"Bucket":"origstore-prod", "Key": f"{hash(video_id)[:4]}/{video_id}/source.mov", "UploadId": upload_id, "PartNumber": n}, ExpiresIn=900) for n in range(1, 64)
]

steps.title: Postgres records UPLOADING row
steps.action: Single-row INSERT into videos with status=UPLOADING and source_ref pointing at the eventual S3 key. Committed synchronously before API responds — on failure, the whole upload POST fails cleanly.

steps.title: API returns upload session to client
steps.action: Response contains video_id, uploadId, the per-part signed URLs, and a CompleteMultipartUpload callback URL. Client will PUT each chunk directly to S3 (bypassing the API) and call back on completion.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return 201, { "video_id": "vid_7a3f91", "upload_session": { "upload_id": "mpu_VXBsb2FkSWQ", "bucket": "origstore-prod", "key": "7a3f/vid_7a3f91/source.mov", "parts": [ {"partNumber": 1, "signedUrl": "https://origstore-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/...&partNumber=1&uploadId=mpu_...", "size": 5242880}, {"partNumber": 2, "signedUrl": "...&partNumber=2&uploadId=mpu_...", "size": 5242880}, "... 61 more parts..." ], "complete_callback": "/videos/vid_7a3f91/upload/complete", "ttl_sec": 900 }, "status": "UPLOADING"
}

steps.title: LB relays upload session back to client
steps.action: Return path. LB closes the short-lived control-plane connection; the bulk-bytes path is client → S3 direct, never touching this LB.

steps.title: Client begins parallel chunked PUT to original storage
steps.action: Client launches a worker pool with concurrency=5, streams SHA-256 per chunk, and issues parallel PUT /part/N requests against the signed URLs. On failure, retries that single chunk (not the whole file). This is the book's 'parallel upload' + 'GOP-aligned chunking' optimization.

steps.title: Original storage absorbs parallel PUTs, fires ObjectCreated event
steps.action: S3 persists each part against the upload_id. Prefix hash (7a3f/) spreads load across partitions, avoiding the 3500 PUT/s per-prefix ceiling. On CompleteMultipartUpload, S3 assembles parts into one object and emits a single s3:ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload event to EventBridge/SNS.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# per-part PUT
PUT /7a3f/vid_7a3f91/source.mov?partNumber=1&uploadId=mpu_VXBsb2FkSWQ
Content-Length: 5242880
#... body bytes...
# → 200 OK, ETag: "a1b2c3..." # after all 63 parts ack'd, client POSTs Complete
POST /7a3f/vid_7a3f91/source.mov?uploadId=mpu_VXBsb2FkSWQ
<CompleteMultipartUpload> <Part><PartNumber>1</PartNumber><ETag>"a1b2c3..."</ETag></Part>...63 parts...
</CompleteMultipartUpload> # S3 emits event:
{ "eventName": "ObjectCreated:CompleteMultipartUpload", "bucket": "origstore-prod", "key": "7a3f/vid_7a3f91/source.mov", "size": 327155712, "etag": "final-assembled-etag", "time": "2026-04-24T10:12:34Z"
}
steps.note: The ObjectCreated event is picked up by the transcode worker pool (see 'transcode' operation). Upload flow does NOT wait for transcode to finish.

steps.title: Client calls complete-upload callback on the API
steps.action: After all 63 parts acked and S3 CompleteMultipartUpload succeeded, the client POSTs to the API's complete_callback so the backend can flip the row to TRANSCODING and enqueue a backup transcode-start message (belt-and-suspenders vs. the S3 event path).

steps.title: LB routes complete-callback to upload-path API
steps.action: Same upload pool; reuses TLS session from the initial POST.

steps.title: API transitions row UPLOADING → TRANSCODING, enqueues backup kickoff
steps.action: API UPDATEs status to TRANSCODING (idempotent via WHERE status='UPLOADING'), produces a belt-and-suspenders message to the Kafka upload-ready topic (in case the S3 event was dropped), and returns 202 Accepted. The actual transcode may already be running from the S3 event.
steps.note: Two paths kick off transcoding: S3 ObjectCreated event (primary) and Kafka upload-ready (backup). Transcoder dedupes on video_id.

steps.title: LB relays 202 Accepted
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Client shows 'Processing — we'll notify you when ready'
steps.action: Client displays a processing state on the creator dashboard. The video_id is usable (creator can edit title/desc now), but playback will 404 until the completion handler flips status to READY (see transcode operation). End-to-end upload wall-clock for 312MB on typical 25Mbps home upload: ~2–4 minutes; transcode adds another 5–15 minutes async.

operations.title: Transcoding flow (DAG) + completion
operations.name: Transcoding flow (DAG) + completion
operations.description: Transcoding workers pull source from original storage, run the DAG (inspection → per-ladder video/audio encode + thumbnails → assembler → HLS manifests), write outputs to transcoded storage, publish to CDN, emit a completion event. Completion handler flips metadata to READY and warms cache.

steps.title: ObjectCreated event delivered to transcoding worker pool
steps.action: Either the S3 ObjectCreated event (primary) or the Kafka upload-ready message (backup) is consumed by a transcode dispatcher, which claims the job via INSERT... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into a transcode_jobs table (idempotent, dedupes the two kickoff paths).
steps.note: Worker only downloads the source once claim succeeds — avoids duplicate GPU spend when both kickoff paths fire.

steps.title: Worker runs DAG: inspect → per-ladder encode (parallel) → audio + thumbnails → assembler
steps.action: Worker downloads source via ranged GETs (pipelined with encode start), runs ffprobe for inspection, then fans out the DAG: video encoding at 240p/480p/720p/1080p in parallel (NVENC H.264), AAC audio encode, thumbnail extraction at 10%/50%/90% marks. Each node retries up to 3× on failure with exponential backoff.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# step 1: inspect (DAG gate — reject malformed sources before fanning out)
$ ffprobe -v error -print_format json -show_streams -show_format s3://.../source.mov
{ "streams": [ {"codec_type":"video","codec_name":"h264","width":3840,"height":2160,"r_frame_rate":"30/1","duration":"842.04"}, {"codec_type":"audio","codec_name":"aac","sample_rate":"48000","channels":2} ], "format": {"duration":"842.04","size":"327155712"}
} # step 2: parallel per-ladder video encode (DAG fan-out)
# ladder: 240p @ 400kbps
$ ffmpeg -i source.mov -c:v h264_nvenc -preset p4 -b:v 400k -maxrate 480k -bufsize 800k \ -vf scale=426:240 -hls_time 6 -hls_playlist_type vod -hls_segment_filename 'seg_%05d.ts' 240p/index.m3u8
# ladder: 480p @ 1200kbps → 141 segments
# ladder: 720p @ 3000kbps → 141 segments
# ladder: 1080p @ 6000kbps → 141 segments # step 3 (parallel with video encodes): audio
$ ffmpeg -i source.mov -vn -c:a aac -b:a 128k -hls_time 6 audio/index.m3u8 # step 4 (parallel): thumbnails
$ ffmpeg -i source.mov -ss 84 -vframes 1 thumb_320.jpg
$ ffmpeg -i source.mov -ss 421 -vframes 1 thumb_640.jpg
$ ffmpeg -i source.mov -ss 758 -vframes 1 thumb_1280.jpg # step 5: assembler joins outputs, emits master.m3u8
cat > master.m3u8 <<EOF
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:6
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=426x240,CODECS="avc1.42e01e,mp4a.40.2",AUDIO="aac"
240p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1200000,RESOLUTION=854x480,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2",AUDIO="aac"
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3000000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2",AUDIO="aac"
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=6000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2",AUDIO="aac"
1080p/index.m3u8
EOF
steps.decision: Inspection gate PASS (valid H.264/AAC). Per-ladder encodes run in parallel; any one ladder can fail independently and the video still publishes with partial ladders.
steps.note: Book's DAG model: inspection → [video encodes || audio encode || thumbnails] → assembler. Parallel fanout is what keeps a 14-min source under 10-min wall-clock encode on GPU.

steps.title: Assembler writes segments + manifests to transcoded storage (segments first, manifest last)
steps.action: Worker writes all 564 segments + 3 thumbnails via parallel PUTs, waits for every ACK, then writes master.m3u8 and per-ladder index.m3u8 LAST. This ordering guarantees clients never see a manifest that references a 404'd segment. Prefix hash (7a3f/) spreads writes across S3 partitions.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# parallel segment PUTs (concurrency-capped at 32 to stay under per-prefix 3500 PUT/s)
for ladder in ("240p", "480p", "720p", "1080p", "audio"): for n in range(1, 142): s3.put_object( Bucket="tcstore-prod", Key=f"7a3f/vid_7a3f91/{ladder}/seg_{n:05d}.ts", Body=segment_bytes, CacheControl="public, max-age=31536000, immutable" )
wait_all_acks # thumbnails
for thumb in ("thumb_320.jpg", "thumb_640.jpg", "thumb_1280.jpg"): s3.put_object(Bucket="tcstore-prod", Key=f"7a3f/vid_7a3f91/{thumb}", Body=...) # per-ladder index.m3u8
for ladder in ("240p", "480p", "720p", "1080p", "audio"): s3.put_object(Bucket="tcstore-prod", Key=f"7a3f/vid_7a3f91/{ladder}/index.m3u8", Body=ladder_playlist, CacheControl="public, max-age=60") # master.m3u8 LAST
s3.put_object(Bucket="tcstore-prod", Key="7a3f/vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8", Body=master_m3u8, CacheControl="public, max-age=60")
steps.note: Transcoded size ~512MB vs. 312MB source = ~1.6x inflation (multi-ladder overhead). Design budgets 4x long-run (adds HEVC/AV1 ladders later).

steps.title: CDN lazily populates on first playback (pull-through)
steps.action: CDN is NOT pre-warmed for every upload — that would push petabytes/day of cold cache fill. Instead, the first viewer's edge miss pulls segments from tcstore (see play-cold flow). For videos flagged as trending by the recommendation pipeline, a pre-warm job pushes the popular ladders to regional shields proactively.

stateAfter.shield.cache: pre-warmed for first 10 segments of 480p/720p if trending

steps.note: Parallel with the completion queue emit — CDN pre-warm is best-effort and does NOT block the READY transition.

steps.title: Assembler emits completion event to Kafka
steps.action: Worker produces a single terminal completion event keyed by video_id to the transcode-complete topic. Strict per-video ordering ensures retries never overtake a later completion for the same id. Payload is slim — full ladder/thumbnail details are fetchable from tcstore if needed.
steps.codeOrCommand:
kafka.produce( topic="transcode-complete", key="vid_7a3f91", # partition by video_id for ordering value={ "video_id": "vid_7a3f91", "manifest_ref": "s3://tcstore-prod/7a3f/vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8", "cdn_manifest_url": "https://cdn.video.example/vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8", "ladders": [ {"name":"240p","bitrate":400000,"resolution":"426x240","codec":"avc1.42e01e"}, {"name":"480p","bitrate":1200000,"resolution":"854x480","codec":"avc1.4d401f"}, {"name":"720p","bitrate":3000000,"resolution":"1280x720","codec":"avc1.640028"}, {"name":"1080p","bitrate":6000000,"resolution":"1920x1080","codec":"avc1.640028"} ], "thumbnails": ["thumb_320.jpg","thumb_640.jpg","thumb_1280.jpg"], "duration_sec": 842, "codec_set": ["h264","aac"], "status": "READY", "assembler_version": "tcw-2026.04", "ts": "2026-04-24T10:20:42Z" }, acks="all" # durable before proceeding
)
steps.note: Durable commit (acks=all) before the worker releases the job — decouples 'encode finished' from 'metadata flipped'.

steps.title: Completion handler consumes event, processes idempotently
steps.action: Handler consumer group drains partition 17, deserializes the event, and begins the two-step finalization: (1) UPDATE metadata DB, (2) write-through cache. Uses at-least-once semantics with idempotency guard WHERE status!= 'READY'.
steps.codeOrCommand: for event in consumer.poll: video_id = event.key payload = event.value # step 1: idempotent DB update rows = db.exec(""" UPDATE videos SET status='READY', manifest_ref=?, ladders=?::jsonb, duration_sec=?, ready_at=NOW WHERE id=? AND status!= 'READY' RETURNING id, owner_id, title """, payload.manifest_ref, json(payload.ladders), payload.duration_sec, video_id) if rows: # step 2: cache write-through (parallel with downstream fanout) cache_write_through(video_id, rows[0], payload) # step 3: downstream fanout (async, separate topics) kafka.produce("search-index", key=video_id, value=payload) kafka.produce("subscriber-notify", key=rows[0].owner_id, value={"new_video": video_id}) consumer.commit(event.offset)

steps.title: Postgres transitions row TRANSCODING → READY
steps.action: UPDATE applies the READY transition atomically. The WHERE status!= 'READY' guard makes replay safe. ladders JSONB is rewritten in a single TOAST update. Write replicates to read replicas within ~200ms.
steps.codeOrCommand:
UPDATE videos
SET status='READY', manifest_ref='s3://tcstore-prod/7a3f/vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8', ladders='[{"name":"240p","bitrate":400000,"resolution":"426x240"}, {"name":"480p","bitrate":1200000,"resolution":"854x480"}, {"name":"720p","bitrate":3000000,"resolution":"1280x720"}, {"name":"1080p","bitrate":6000000,"resolution":"1920x1080"}]'::jsonb, duration_sec=842, ready_at=NOW
WHERE id='vid_7a3f91' AND status!= 'READY'
RETURNING id, owner_id, title;
steps.note: The watch page will now return status=READY on next fetch. Creator dashboard stops polling.

steps.title: Handler write-throughs Redis (parallel with downstream fanout)
steps.action: Handler writes the fresh metadata blob to Redis with 5-min TTL — write-through avoids the miss window that a DEL-then-populate pattern would create. Runs in parallel with the search-index + subscriber-notify fanout so DB commit doesn't block on them.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# write-through (NOT del) to eliminate miss window
cache.setex( f"video:vid_7a3f91", 300, # 5 min TTL json.dumps({ "id": "vid_7a3f91", "title": "Distributed Systems Patterns", "status": "READY", "manifest_ref": "cdn://vid_7a3f91/master.m3u8", "ladders": ["240p","480p","720p","1080p"], "duration_sec": 842, "owner_id": "usr_creator_11", "version": 7 })
) # cross-region pub/sub invalidation (fanout to other regional caches)
redis.publish("video.invalidations", {"video_id": "vid_7a3f91", "version": 7})
steps.note: End-to-end: user's upload POST happened ~8 minutes ago. Next watch-page load hits cache, player starts CDN segment flow, video is live. The book's full parallel-upload + async-transcode + completion-queue pattern is now complete.

tradeoffs.rationale: Pushing 95%+ of segment bytes to edge PoPs is the only way to serve ~115K QPS globally under 100 ms P99 without a multi-Tbps origin. Origin cost and failure blast radius both shrink dramatically.

tradeoffs.chosen: Async DAG of workers with a completion queue
tradeoffs.rationale: A 10-minute encode cannot block the upload response. Async keeps the 'processing' UX simple and lets the encoder fleet scale independently; cost is a delay before the video is watchable.

tradeoffs.chosen: Full ABR ladder (6-8 renditions) per source
tradeoffs.rationale: Trades ~4x raw storage for adaptive playback across 2G phones to 1 Gbps fiber. Cheaper than re-encoding on demand and keeps the edge cache-friendly.

tradeoffs.chosen: Resumable multipart with 5 MB GOP-aligned chunks
tradeoffs.rationale: Avoids restarting multi-GB uploads on a single flaky connection and allows parallel PUTs to saturate the user's uplink. Adds server bookkeeping for part manifests.
Video metadata is relational (owner, ACL, playlists) and read-dominated. SQL gives transactional updates on privacy changes; Redis absorbs the 10-100x read amplification.
